item.content:encoded:
Indian VCs And The Deeptech Dilemma

Skyroot has proved that homegrown startups can build rockets, but the bigger challenge may lie in funding them. A recent viral critique of Indian venture capitalists has reignited the debate over deeptech funding gaps, risk appetite of investors and slow diligence. 

Founder Grievances: For many early stage founders, deeptech funding in India remains plagued by prolonged due diligence, demands for commercial traction before validation and an over-reliance on founder pedigree. Their criticism is aimed at the current system, which may be underwriting very little genuine technological risk and backing a handful of startups.

Concentration Problem: Data adds further nuance to the debate. Deeptech funding surged 176% YoY in Q3 2026, but the deal count barely moved. This is because most of the capital was heavily concentrated among a few players and that too in Bengaluru. The pattern suggests that the capital is largely flowing to technically validated companies, while early stage founders pursuing unproven scientific experiments still struggle to secure their first cheque.

Why Investors Hesitate? Indian VCs have historically been hesitant towards deeptech bets due to the sector’s long gestation cycles, uncertain exits, specialised diligence and substantial follow-on capital. Venture funds also operate under pressure from limited partners to mint returns and liquidity within defined timelines. As a result, most VCs hesitate to underwrite these uncertain scientific bets.

Changing Ecosystem: However, the picture is not entirely bleak. Founder-led vehicles and specialist funds are expanding and raising big bucks for moonshots. Government initiatives, like the ₹1 Lakh Cr RDI Fund, are also creating more optimism around deeptech. But capital alone will not solve the problem as local frontier ventures still need stronger follow-on funding, patient limited partners and the corporate willing to buy early products.

Indian founders have proved that they can build rockets, but can VCs now step in and show that they can finance these moonshot bets? Let’s find out…

From The Editor’s Desk

Weekly Funding Rundown 

  • Indian startups cumulatively raised $130.2 Mn last week, down 29% from $184 Mn in the preceding week. However, deal count zoomed 88% week-on-week to 32. Cent and Simplismart took the biggest cheques home at $15 Mn and $14 Mn, respectively.
  • Ecommerce emerged as the most funded sector last week, bagging $33 Mn across nine deals. Following suit were AI ventures, which bagged $30 Mn across five deals. 
  • On the investor front, Blume Ventures and Antler emerged as the most active investors last week and backed three startups each.

E2W Sales In October

  • Electric two-wheeler registrations grew a marginal 2.9% month-on-month to 2.1 Lakh units in October. Sales also rose 48% YoY from 1.4 Lakh units a year earlier. 
  • Legacy giants TVS Motor and Hero MotoCorp recorded gains and improved their market share to 27.2% and 13.4%, respectively. However, Bajaj Auto reported a decline in sales in October, which led to its market share falling to 21.7% from 23.4% in September.
  • Growth also tapered off for new-age EV makers in October. Ather’s registrations declined 1.8% to 30,380 units from 30,942 units in September, while its market share slipped to 14.2%. Ola Electric’s sales also tanked 13.7% MoM to 11,614 units last month. 

Kickback Allegations At Flipkart

  • Walmart has launched a probe into allegations that employees at the ecommerce giant received over ₹150 Cr in kickbacks from vendors. The charges have been directed against employees in Flipkart’s smartphones and luggage and travel accessories divisions.
  • The complaints allege the certain employees accepted payments and favours from vendors in exchange for preferential treatment on the ecommerce platform, including greater visibility that helped drive sales.
  • This is Walmart’s third investigation into alleged financial misconduct at Flipkart in the past three years. A previous probe resulted in three dismissals two-and-a-half years ago, while another investigation found wrongdoing by an employee barely six months ago.

eMudhra & Accountability

  • The cybersecurity firm came under fire last month after researchers discovered that its private keys were weak and could be recovered in under a second. The row saw eMudhra exit the global TLS certificate business altogether. 
  • The episode demonstrates that global browser makers, rather than local regulators, became the first line of accountability for eMudhra. This raises a governance question for India: who investigates and prevents a similar failure domestically?
  • Experts now flag that eMudhra’s exit means that Indian websites may increasingly depend on foreign certificate authorities for trust. This could affect India’s digital sovereignty and its ability to build a domestic public-key infrastructure ecosystem.

Bullish Week For Startup Stocks

  • Of the 69 new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage, 40 gained between 0.2% and 26.8%, last week. However, the remaining 29 declined by up to 22.3%. Startup stocks largely saw gains as quarterly earnings drove sharp moves in individual counters. 
  • Ather Energy and Zetwerk emerged as the biggest gainers, while shares of CarTrade and AceVector shed the most. The combined market-cap of these 69 stocks jumped to $160.9 Bn at the end of last week, up 5.7% from $152.3 Bn in the week-ago period.
  • Going forward, investors will track the upcoming US midterm elections, Brent crude oil prices, geopolitical developments and quarterly earnings for market cues this week.

upliance.ai Eyes $4 Mn

  • The D2C home appliance maker in advanced talks to raise $3 Mn to $4 Mn in its Series A round. The fundraise will likely see participation from a fresh investor, while existing backers, including Khosla Ventures, will also double down.
  • Founded in 2021, upliance.ai sells AI-powered kitchen appliances like food processors and air fryers. The D2C brand had last raised ₹34 Cr in a seed round led by Khosla Ventures in 2024 at a valuation of ₹143 Cr.
  • The development comes amid growing activity in India’s smart kitchen appliances market, which is being driven by growing demand for automated products and rising disposable incomes. The space is projected to become a $3 Bn opportunity by 2032.

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

How D-Propulse Is Rethinking Jet Engines

India has pursued indigenous jet-engine capability for decades now, but to no avail. This has created heavy dependence on overseas vendors and costly testing. D-Propulse is betting on a new technology to build lighter, cheaper propulsion for high-speed drones and missiles.

The RDE Approach: Founded in 2025, D-Propulse is developing rotating detonation engines (RDEs), which use supersonic detonation waves to generate thrust. It has already tested a 5 kN air-breathing RDE that is currently at technology readiness level-5. The startup claims its engine will be 15-25% more efficient and at least 60% less expensive than conventional ramjets.

Eye On The Prize: To scale its ambitions, the startup is also building a 5,000+ sq ft combustor test facility at IIT Madras, with air mass flow capacity of around 10 kg/sec and an in-house HPC cluster. It is also exploring infrastructure rental as an early revenue stream while its jet engine business takes shape.

Building For Defence: D-Propulse is targeting the Indian Armed Forces as its intended first customers. It now plans to conduct flight tests between June and December 2027 and limited series production by the end of 2028. The pre-revenue startup also plans to raise a Series A round by early next year.

With the global RDE opportunity projected to surpass $2.4 Bn by 2030, can D-Propulse build commercially viable jet engines for India?

item.title: Two Point O Bags $10 Mn To Bridge The Financing Gap In Clean Energy
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: India’s clean energy transition is attracting significant capital, but much of it is flowing into utility-scale projects. Smaller installations across…
item.content:encoded:
India’s clean energy transition is attracting significant capital, but much of it is flowing into utility-scale projects. Smaller installations across factories, commercial buildings and industrial facilities continue to face a financing gap, even when the technology is commercially viable and can help businesses lower operating costs.

Two Point O Capital wants to channel capital into this underserved segment by bringing financing, technology and project execution under one platform.

To fuel its ambition, the startup has now raised $10 Mn (nearly ₹95 Cr) in its Series A round led by Transition Venture Capital (TVC). The round also saw participation from existing backer Omnivore and angel investors Chiranjeev Singh Saluja and Sudhir M Reddy.

The startup plans to utilise a major chunk of the fresh proceeds towards financing the deployment of clean energy assets for its commercial and industrial (C&I) customers. The capital will also be utilised to strengthen the startup’s tech stack and ramp up hiring.

The latest round comes two years after Two Point O raised over $6 Mn, via a mix of equity and debt, in 2024 .

“There was a lot of capital that was getting pumped into utility-scale, grid-scale projects. But there wasn’t enough capital inflows into the distributed or decentralised energy projects, to put it simply, for industries and buildings,” cofounder and CEO Karan Bhutani told Inc42.

Founded in 2024 by Bhutani, Archit Mehrotra, Manya Ranjan and Shashidhar Reddy, Two Point O provides financing, turnkey solutions and equipment leasing across areas such as rooftop solar, battery energy storage systems (BESS) and wastewater treatment. Unlike traditional banks and NBFCs, the startup claims to be focused on smaller-scale projects.

Building A Full-Stack Clean Energy Platform

Two Point O positions itself as a full-stack clean energy enablement platform for commercial and industrial (C&I) customers. Its offerings span four asset classes:

  • Rooftop Solar: Distributed solar installations for commercial and industrial facilities
  • BESS: Solutions to optimise energy consumption and manage peak demand
  • Energy Efficiency: Upgrades across heating, cooling and air compressors
  • Wastewater treatment: Projects to improve water treatment and resource utilisation

The startup offers multiple financing structures. It operates a wholly-owned NBFC subsidiary, which handles loan disbursals, while a separate operating entity caters to lease and service-based requirements.

Bhutani also claims that the startup has built a proprietary underwriting engine that uses technology to assess a project’s technical specifications, performance and credit profiles. This allows Two Point O to dish out a techno-commercial proposal for a client within 24 to 48 hours, he added.

Two Point O also monitors assets after deployment. Bhutani said that all deployed assets are IoT-enabled, with real-time data used for preventive maintenance, performance optimisation and verification.

Notably, the startup does not directly undertake installation and maintenance. Instead, it relies on original equipment manufacturers as well as engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) partners for execution, and oversees them through technology and contracts. Bhutani said that this “light-touch” model gives the startup the ability to scale its operations.

Inside Two Point O’s Cross-Selling Model

India’s clean tech market, as per IMARC Group, could become a $95 Bn opportunity by 2034. Two Point O is eyeing a much smaller piece of this market as it operates at the intersection of lending tech and B2B clean energy enablement segments. 

To carve a niche in the space, Two Point O has so far focused on roping in big-ticket clients and cross-selling additional solutions to these customers. This approach, as per Bhutani, allows the startup to keep customer acquisition costs low and get more out of its users. 

So far, the startup claims to have already onboarded around 25-30 large customers, including Premier Energies, Godrej, JK Tyre, Morepen Pharma, Wipro and Phoenix Mills. Bhutani estimates that its existing customer base could generate ₹400-500 Cr in transactions over the next two to three years. The startup also noted that its assets under management (AUM) grew 1.5X sequentially in each of the last three quarters.

Not stopping there, the startup has much more in store going forward:

  • Enter the SME segment and expand across India
  • Build an AUM of $75 Mn to $100 Mn over the next couple of years
  • Expand into new sectors like data centres, automotives, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing and healthcare

Inc42 Take: Can Two Point O Scale Its Multi-Asset Model?

Two Point O is addressing a financing gap in distributed clean energy by combining capital, technology and project execution. What works for the startup is its multi-asset model, which could help deepen relationships with existing customers and generate repeat business.

However, scaling across asset classes will require strong underwriting, consistent asset performance and effective oversight of operating partners. The planned SME expansion also brings additional challenges around technology risks, regulations and credit assessment.

The startup’s ability to turn its customer base and growing AUM into sustained revenue and profitability remains to be seen, particularly as it expands its portfolio and deployment commitments.

item.content:encoded:
Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets.

The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership.

Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. 

“⁠Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership.

Building on the momentum, seventeen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. 

Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty five startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO and Razorpay alone could raise nearly ₹20,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs.

However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. 

“IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42.

There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation.

Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub.

Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026

AceVector

Founded by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, AceVector traces its roots to 2010, when the duo founded ecommerce platform Snapdeal. Over the years, this umbrella company expanded to include listed ecommerce enablement startup Unicommerce and house of brands Stellaro Brands.

The three companies unified under the AceVector banner in 2022. Now, three years on, the consolidated entity is gearing up for a public market debut.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, AceVector filed its confidential DRHP with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in July 2025. The regulator greenlit the offering in November 2025.

Almost a year later in September 2026, AceVector filed its red herring prospectus with the SEBI, which outlined a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS component of up to 4.16 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per share, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. 

Subsequently, AceVector’s public issue was oversubscribed 4.93X, receiving bids for 36.61 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer. 

The company eventually made a weak debut on the exchanges on October 5. Shares of AceVector listed at ₹28.30 on the BSE, a discount of 11.6% to its issue price of ₹32 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹28.32, an 11.5% discount to the IPO price.

On the financial front, AceVector’s operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹395 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, losses also shrank nearly 64% to ₹45.5 Cr versus ₹126.3 Cr in FY25.

Amagi 

Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. 

The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services.

The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares.

Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. 

The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price.

Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr.

Aye Finance

Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO.

In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. 

Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr.

The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses, listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. 

On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. 

ESDS Software Solution

Founded in 2005 by Piyush Somani, ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. It operates five data centres in Navi Mumbai, Nashik, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Noida.

The data centre company claims to have served 2,501 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with an average revenue per customer of around ₹19 Lakh.

Backed by ace investor Ashish Kacholia, ESDS Software Solution has raised nearly $47.3 Mn in funding to date. 

ESDS first attempted to go public in September 2021 but the plan failed to materialise due to aftershocks of the pandemic. The company then refiled its papers in March 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in December 2025.

As per its RHP, ESDS Software Solution’s public issue consisted solely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹720 Cr. 

Its public issue, which stretched between August 28 and September 1, closed with an oversubscription of 135.88X. Subsequently, shares of the company made a stellar debut on the bourses, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over the issue price of ₹429.

On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹746.30, marking a gain of nearly 74% over the issue price. 

On the financial front, the company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹120.8 Cr in FY26, up 117% from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25.

Fractal 

Founded in 2000 by Srikanth Velamakanni, Pranay Agrawal, and Ashwath Bhat, Fractal is a SaaS unicorn that offers AI-powered analytics solutions to enterprises globally. 

Backed by TPG Capital, Khazanah Nasional, and Apax Partners, the startup has raised $800 Mn to date. It achieved unicorn status in 2022 and was last valued at more than $2 Bn.

In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI, and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025. The company’s ₹2,833.9 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,023.54 Cr and an OFS worth up to ₹1,810.4 Cr. 

The public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.66X, with investors placing bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 1.86 Cr on offer. Fractal’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the exchanges and listed at ₹876 on the NSE, a discount of 2.7% to the issue price of ₹900. On the BSE, the shares listed flat at ₹900.

On the financial front, Fractal’s profit declined about 3% YoY to ₹70.9 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹1,559 Cr. 

Kissht

Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a digital lending platform that offers personal and business loans up to ₹5 Lakh. It uses AI and machine learning to assess creditworthiness. It also offers health insurance products and credit against property.

The startup has secured over $140 Mn till date from investors such as Vertex Growth, Brunei Investment Agency, Endiya Partners, and Ventureast.

 The lending tech startup filed its DRHP in August last year and received SEBI’s nod to proceed with its public listing in January 2026. 

As per its RHP, its IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹850 Cr and an OFS component of up to 44.4 Lakh shares. It had set a price band of ₹162-₹171 for the public issue, which was oversubscribed 9.5X.

Subsequently, Kissht made a stellar debut on the bourses on May 8. The lending tech startup’s shares listed at ₹191 a piece on the BSE, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price of ₹171. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹190, up 11.1% from the issue price.

On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹199.3 Cr in 9M FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹1,569.9 Cr during the period under review. 

Klassroom

Founded in 2016 by the mother-sons trio of Alka, Dhruv, and Dhumil Javeri, Klassroom is an edtech startup that operates at the intersection of offline and online coaching. It operates 30 offline partner centres that cater to both academic and skill-development needs. 

It also collaborates with state governments, private companies and education institutions to deliver academic and skilling programmes. The edtech startup also offers an AI-powered education OTT app that features over 100 courses for classes 8 to 12, and claims to have a footprint of over 4 Lakh registered users across the country.

The startup raised over $2 Mn in private rounds from the likes of actor Suniel Shetty, ah! Ventures, LetsVenture, CPT Family Trust, Growth Sense and others.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings in February 2026, Klassroom filed its DRHP with the BSE for an SME IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to 19.89 Lakh shares and an OFS component of up to 4.66 Lakh shares. The startup subsequently received the in-principle approval from BSE to move ahead with its public offering in May 2026. 

It had set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for the issue, looking to raise ₹39 Cr at a valuation of ₹148.1 Cr. Subsequently, the startup’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 1.46X.

Shares of Klassroom listed on the BSE SME on August 7 at ₹170, a premium of 6.92% to the issue price of ₹159. With this, the company became the second listed edtech startup in the country, after PhysicsWallah. 

On the financial front, Klassroom posted an operating revenue of ₹23 Cr in FY26, up 128% from around ₹10 Cr in the year prior. Meanwhile, net profit jumped nearly 162% to ₹7.6 Cr from ₹2.9 Cr in FY25.

LEAP India

A brainchild of Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions through asset pooling, enabling companies to share pallets, containers, and other assets. 

Founded in 2013, the platform also offers inventory management, transportation, returnable packaging and tool repair. It also sells electric and fossil fuel-powered forklifts through its subsidiary TRON.

LEAP India has raised over $184 Mn till date from investors like KKR and Sixth Sense Ventures.

The startup first attempted to list on the bourses in 2022, eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr listing. But the plan was later shelved amid market volatility.

Reigniting its IPO plans, the logistics tech startup then filed its DRHP with SEBI in August 2025, and received SEBI’s nod in December 2025. 

In August 2026, the company filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹480 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹2,000 Cr. 

The company then set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for its public issue, which eventually closed with an oversubscription of 8.38X as investors bid for 96.32 Cr shares as against 11.49 Cr shares on offer.

Shares of LEAP India eventually made their debut on the bourses on August 14, listing at a premium of about 4.4% to the issue price of ₹159. The stock got listed at ₹166 on the BSE and ₹165.90 on the NSE.

Financially, LEAP India’s net profits zoomed 65.3% to ₹62.3 Cr in FY26 as against ₹37.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue climbed 56.4% to ₹729.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹466.5 Cr in FY25.

Moneyview

Founded in 2016 by Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, Moneyview started off as a personal finance platform before pivoting to digital lending. Today, it offers services such as UPI payments, gold SIPs, fixed deposits, digital gold, home loans, BNPL and insurance.

The company claims to manage over  ₹19,800 Cr in AUM and has raised more than $250 Mn in funding. It competes with players like listed fintech MobiKwik, IPO-aspirant Navi, and MoneyTap. It entered the unicorn club in 2024.

In March 2026, the fintech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO. It then received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in late-June 2026.

In September 2026, the fintech unicorn filed its RHP. outlining an IPO with a fresh issue of shares worth ₹750 Cr and an OFS component of up to 10.04 Cr equity shares. The startup’s public issue then closed with an oversubscription of 98.46X, led by QIBs and NIIs. 

The digital lender made a bumper debut on the exchanges on October 1, with its shares listing at ₹55.6 on the BSE, a premium of 64% over the issue price of ₹34. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹55, marking a premium of nearly 62% over the issue price. 

Moneyview’s operating revenue grew 43.3% to ₹3,351.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,339.1 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, net profit rose a marginal 1% to ₹242.7 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹240.3 Cr in FY25.

Purple Style Labs

Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs is an omnichannel luxury house of brands featuring fashion labels like Pernia’s Pop Up Studio & Shop, Wendell Rodricks, and Hemant Trevedi. It operates over 12 Pernia’s Pop-Up Studio experience centres across India.

Backed by Alchemy Capital Management, Bajaj Holdings and Investment, and Minerva Ventures, the startup has raised more than $78 Mn to date.

In September 2025, the D2C brand filed its DRHP with SEBI for its public issue and received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. 

It then filed its RHP with SEBI in August 2026 for a public issue, which consisted entirely of a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹680 Cr, with no offer for sale component. 

Subsequently, Purple Style Labs’ public issue opened for subscription in late August 2026 and closed with an oversubscription of 1.29X, receiving bids for 88.54 Lakh shares against 68.49 Lakh shares on offer. 

Shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on September 7. The stock listed at ₹535 on the NSE, 6.96% lower than the issue price of ₹575. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹539, representing a discount of 6.26%.

On the financial front, the startup’s consolidated net loss widened 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26 as against ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue for the fiscal rose nearly 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in FY25.

RentoMojo 

Founded in 2014 by Geetansh Bamania and Ajay Nain, RentoMojo is an omnichannel rental platform to lease appliances, furniture, and furnishings. The startup operates an app, website and physical stores. It operates 20 warehouses and 82 offline stores across 29 cities. 

Backed by Accel, Chiratae Ventures and Bain Capital, the startup has raised over $45 Mn in funding to date.

Hopping on the IPO bandwagon in March 2026, the rental platform filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO and received SEBI’s nod to float its public issue in July 2026.

In September 2026, the startup finally filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.7 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹384-₹404 per share for its IPO.

The public issue opened for bidding on September 9 and closed on September 11. The IPO was oversubscribed 72.88X, receiving bids for 158.68 Cr shares against the 2.18 Cr shares on offer.

Shares of RentoMojo made a strong stock market debut on September 17. The stock listed at ₹482.45 on the NSE, a premium of 19.42% over its issue price of ₹404. On the BSE, RentoMojo opened at ₹480, up 18.81% from the issue price.

The IPO opened despite RentoMojo cofounder and former COO Nain earlier filing a petition before the NCLT’s Bengaluru bench to stall the IPO proceedings. 

Alleging oppression and mismanagement, the plea claimed that incomplete or inaccurate information was shared with him and sought to declare his 2023 sale of 2,223 shares void ab initio.

On the financial front, RentoMojo reported a profit after tax of ₹104.3 Cr in FY26, up 142% from ₹43.1 Cr in the previous fiscal, aided by a tax credit of ₹36.6 Cr. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 45.5% to ₹387 Cr during the year under review from ₹266 Cr in FY25. 

SEDEMAC

Founded in 2007 by IIT-Bombay professor Shashikanth Suryanarayana and his students Pushkaraj Panse, Amit Dixit, and Manish Sharma, SEDMAC designs electronic control systems for mobility and industrial applications.

The deeptech company produces motor control units, integrated starter generators, fuel injection systems, genset controllers, and small industrial powertrains. Backed by Xponentia Capital Partners, A91 Partners, and 360 ONE Asset, SEDMAC has raised over $107 Mn to date.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the deeptech company filed its DRHP with SEBI in November 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in February 2026. 

Its public issue comprised solely an OFS component of up to 80.43 Lakh shares. The IPO was oversubscribed 2.68X, with investors cumulatively bidding for 1.51 Cr shares against 56.32 Lakh shares on offer.

Shares of the company made a stellar debut on the exchanges on March 11, listing at a premium of 13.5% on the NSE. The stock opened at ₹1,535 as against the issue price of ₹1,352 per share. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹1,510, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price.

SEDEMAC reported a net profit of ₹71.4 Cr in the first nine months of FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹770.66 Cr during the period under review. 

Shadowfax

Founded in 2015 by Vaibhav Khandelwal and Abhishek Bansal, Shadowfax is a logistics company that offers hyperlocal and on-demand delivery solutions for businesses.

Competing with the likes of Delhivery, LoadShare and Pickrr, the logistics major is backed by names such as Flipkart, Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India), IFC, Nokia Growth Partners, Qualcomm and Trifecta Capital.

Shadowfax pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 for an IPO, and received markets regulator’s nod in October 2025. It filed its updated DRHP with SEBI in November 2025. The company’s IPO comprised a fresh issue worth ₹1,000 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹907 Cr. 

The company’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.72X, receiving total bids for 24.23 Cr shares against 8.9 Cr on offer. 

Subsequently, shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on January 28. The stock listed at ₹112.60 apiece on the NSE, a discount of 9.19% to the issue price of ₹124. On the BSE, shares of the logistics unicorn debuted at ₹113, down 8.87% below the issue price. 

In H1 FY26, the logistics unicorn’s net profit more than doubled to ₹21 Cr from ₹9.8 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue surged 68.4% YoY to ₹1,805.6 Cr during the period.

Shiprocket

Founded in 2017 by Saahil Goel, Vishesh Khurana, Akshay Gulati, and Gautam Kapoor, Shiprocket aggregates third-party logistics providers. It claims to partner 17 courier firms like Delhivery, FedEx, Aramex, Xpressbees, DTDC, and Shadowfax and serves over 24,000 pin codes across India.

The logistics unicorn has raised over $323 Mn to date from investors like Temasek, Bertelsmann, Tribe Capital, Lightrock, and Zomato.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the Zomato-backed unicorn in May 2025 confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI and received the regulator’s approval in October 2025. Shiprocket then filed its RHP with the markets regulator in August 2026.

The logistics major’s ₹1,617 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹885.5 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹732 Cr. 

Subsequently, in mid-August 2026, Shiprocket’s public issue opened to healthy market response and closed with an oversubscription of 99.38X, receiving bidding for 938.53 Cr shares against 9.44 Cr shares on offer. 

Shares of the company made a strong debut on the D-Street on August 19. The stock listed at ₹131 on the NSE, marking a premium of 35.05% to the issue price of ₹97. On the BSE, it debuted at ₹129.50, a premium of 33.51%.  

On the financial front, Shiprocket’s operating revenue rose 24% to ₹2,024 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,632 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, net loss widened over 6% to ₹79.2 Cr during the fiscal from ₹74.5 Cr in FY25.

Tonbo Imaging

Founded in 2012 by Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D’Souza, Tonbo Imaging is a defence tech startup that designs and builds advanced imaging and sensor systems. Its product portfolio includes smart thermal weapon sights, see-through armors, AI-based seekers, and gun shock simulators.

The company has raised over $59 Mn to date from investors such as Artiman Ventures, Celesta Capital, and Qualcomm Ventures. It counts NATO, US Navy SEALs, Israeli Defense Forces and the defence ministries of India and Armenia as its customers.

After initially filing its DRHP with SEBI in December 2025, the startup once again filed fresh draft papers with the market regulator in August 2026, eyeing an IPO consisting solely of an OFS component of 1.81 Cr shares. It received SEBI’s nod in September 2026. 

The defence tech startup’s public issue opened to healthy investor enthusiasm and was oversubscribed 135.8X. Shares of Tonbo Imaging eventually made a strong stock market debut and listed at ₹1,162 on the BSE, a 66% premium to its issue price of ₹700 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹1,160, translating into a listing gain of 65.71%. 

Tonbo’s net profit declined 30% to ₹362.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹469.1 Cr in the previous year. Operating revenue slumped 22.7% to ₹299.9 Cr from ₹374.3 Cr in FY25.

Turtlemint

Founded in 2015 by Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and Anand Prabhudesai, Turtlemint operates an insurtech platform that enables financial advisors to distribute car, bike, health, and term life insurance to their customer networks. It claims to serve over 3 Lakh advisors nationwide.

The startup has raised more than $197 Mn to date from investors such as Amansa Capital, Jungle Ventures, Peak XV Partners, Vitruvian Partners, and Nexus Venture Partners.

In September 2025, Turtlemint pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI, and secured market regulator’s approval three months later in December.

Subsequently, the insurtech unicorn filed its RHP in June 2026. The IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹660.7 Cr and an OFS of 1.46 Cr shares.

Its public issue opened on June 19 and closed on June 23, with an oversubscription of 1.2X.

Despite this, the startup made a muted debut on the bourses on June 29. 

Shares of the insurtech startup listed at ₹134.90 on the NSE, a discount of 11.25% to the issue price of ₹152. On the BSe, the stock listed at ₹136.2 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 10.4% to the issue price.

The insurtech company’s net loss rose 19% to ₹184.7 Cr in the first nine months (9M) of FY26 as against a net loss of ₹154.7 Cr in the year-ago period. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 80% to ₹741.1 Cr from ₹411.1 Cr in 9M FY25.

Zetwerk

Founded in 2018 by Amrit Acharya, Srinath Ramakkrushnan, Rahul Sharma and Vishal Chaudhary, Zetwerk operates a B2B platform that connects manufacturers with vendors and suppliers of industrial machine components.

The unicorn has so far raised over $793 Mn to date from the likes of Greenoaks Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Mars Growth Capital and Peak XV Partners.

The startup first kicked off its IPO plans in February 2025 as it began lining up bankers for its public issue. Zetwerk later dialed back the plans and postponed its listing. By November 2025, Zetwerk reversed its course again and appointed six bankers to helm its IPO. 

In August 2026, the unicorn filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for its public issue, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹2,600 Cr and an OFS component of up to 9.6 Cr equity shares. 

The issue finally opened for subscription on October 15 and closed on October 19 with an oversubscription of 3.06X. Shares of the unicorn listed at ₹159.25 on the NSE, a premium of 5.46% to its issue price of ₹151. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹159, up 5.3% from the issue price. 

Zetwerk’s revenue from operations zoomed over 40% to ₹15,913.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹11,300 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, net loss climbed 333% to ₹1,606.1 Cr during the fiscal under review from ₹370.7 Cr in FY25.

Startups That Have Filed DRHP 

Atomberg

Founded in 2012 by Manoj Meena and Sibabrata Das, Atomberg began as a B2B supplier of energy-efficient BLDC fans before entering the D2C segment in 2016. It has since expanded to manufacture mixer grinders, water purifiers, and small appliances. 

The startup designs and manufactures its products in India and sells them via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. Backed by names such as Steadview Capital, Jungle Ventures and A91 Partners, Atomberg has raised over $126 Mn in funding to date.

Taking the first step towards its public listing, the D2C appliance brand, in July 2026, converted into a public entity and changed the name of its parent entity from Atomberg Technologies Pvt Ltd to Atomberg Technologies Ltd.

In August 2026, the startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹450 Cr and an OFS of up to 7.65 Cr shares. The startup is also considering raising up to ₹90 Cr through a pre-IPO placement. 

On the financial front, Atomberg’s losses widened 26.5% to ₹149 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹117.8 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 34.8% to ₹1,293.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹959.5 Cr in FY25.

AVPL International (AITMC Ventures)

Founded in 2016 by Preet Sandhuu and Deep Sisai, AITMC sits at the intersection of agriculture and drones. It manufactures drones, offers drone-as-a-service, and runs more than 70 drone training centres across 16 states.

In July 2025, AITMC kicked off its IPO plans once again as the company’s board approved a proposal to increase the fresh issue size of its IPO to ₹200 Cr from ₹125 Cr previously. 

AITMC then filed its draft papers with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in October 2025. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026.

In September 2026, the drone tech startup filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which consists solely of a fresh issue of up to 3.5 Cr shares. 

Notably, this marks its second attempt at going public. Previously in December 2023, the company was eyeing an NSE Emerge listing, which comprised solely of a fresh issue of up to 2.1 Cr shares.

That earlier plan was shelved after AITMC signed a term sheet in January 2025 for a strategic merger with BSE SME-listed DroneAcharya, a deal that ultimately fell through.

On the financial front, AITMC Ventures’ net profit climbed 59% to ₹14 Cr in FY25 from ₹8.8 Cr a fiscal earlier, while operating revenue zoomed 87% to ₹87.5 Cr as against ₹46.8 Cr in FY24.

boAt

Founded in 2016 by Aman Gupta and Sameer Mehta, boAt is a D2C consumer electronics brand that sells headphones, smartwatches, speakers, and other audio wearables.

The company has raised over $171 Mn across multiple rounds from investors such as Warburg Pincus, Qualcomm Ventures, Malabar Investments, Innoven Capital, and Fireside Ventures.

boAt has pursued an IPO for several years now. It first filed its DRHP with SEBI in 2022 for a ₹2,000 Cr public issue, but later shelved the plan amid challenging market conditions.

Taking a second shot, the boAt’s parent, Imagine Marketing, pre-filed its DRHP confidentially with the SEBI in April 2025, and secured SEBI approval in August. 

In October 2025, boAt filed its updated DRHP for an ₹1,500 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to ₹500 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹1,000 Cr.

On the financial front, boAt saw its revenue from operations grow 10.7% YoY to ₹628.1 Cr in Q1 FY26, while profit stood at ₹21.3 Cr compared to a ₹31 Cr loss in Q1 FY25.

Burma Burma

Founded in 2013 by Ankit Gupta and Chirag Chhajer, Hunger Pangs operates the Burma Burma chain of casual dining restaurants. The chain serves vegetarian Burmese cuisine and runs 22 restaurants and a delivery kitchen across nine cities, including Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Delhi NCR.

The startup has raised more than $11 Mn in funding to date and competes against the likes of names such as Mainland China, Mamagoto, Yum Yum Cha, and Berco’s.

The company’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Pvt Ltd, filed its DRHP with markets regulator SEBI in October 2026. Its public issue comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹150 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.8 Cr shares.

C5i 

Founded in 2000 by Ashwin Mittal, C5i (formerly known as Course5 Intelligence) is an enterprise AI company that helps large businesses automate tasks and turn data into actionable insights.

Backed by names such as Nuvama Asset Management and 360 ONE, the startup has raised more than $55 Mn in funding to date. The platform first attempted to go public in 2022, targeting a ₹600 Cr IPO, but later shelved the plans due to weak market conditions.

Reigniting its IPO ambitions, the startup once again filed its DRHP with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in July 2026. C5i is now looking to raise about ₹1,000-1,200 Cr via the public issue. 

On the financial front, C5i’s consolidated net profit declined 15% to ₹48.3 Cr in FY25 as against ₹56.7 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile its operating revenue surged 26% to ₹545.3 Cr from ₹431.4 Cr in FY24.

Cult.fit

Founded in 2016 by ex-Myntra cofounder Mukesh Bansal and former Flipkart executive Ankit Nagori (who left in 2020), Cult.fit runs a fitness empire spanning gyms, cloud kitchen Eat.fit, mental wellness platform called Mind.fit, among other verticals. 

Backed by Zomato, Accel, Tata Digital, Temasek, Kalaari Capital, and Chiratae Ventures, the startup has raised over $650 Mn to date.

Joining the IPO wave, Cult.fit filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2026. The startup’s IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹950 Cr and an offer for sale of up to 17.86 Cr shares. As per sources, The total IPO size is likely to be around ₹4,000 Cr.

It received the market regulator’s nod to move ahead within its IPO in October 2026. 

On the financial front, the unicorn managed to narrow its net loss to ₹251.8 Cr in FY26 as against ₹480.8 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 41.5% to ₹1,720.6 Cr in the fiscal under review compared to ₹1,215.5 Cr in FY25. 

Curefoods

Founded in 2020 by Ankit Nagori, Curefoods is a cloud kitchen unicorn that manages brands like EatFit, CakeZone, Nomad Pizza, Sharief Bhai Biryani, and Frozen Bottle.

It claims to operate over 200 cloud kitchens and offline outlets across 70 Indian cities. The startup has raised over $175 Mn from backers including Iron Pillar, Accel, Three State Ventures, Chiratae Ventures, and ASK Finance.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, Curefoods filed its DRHP with SEBI in late June 2025 and received markets regulator’s approval in late October. As per the DRHP, the proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of up to  ₹800 Cr and an offer-for-sale of up to 4.85 Cr equity shares.

However, in June 2026, the startup took a U-turn and put its IPO plans on hold amid the turmoil in the Indian equities market and concerns over its potential valuation. As per reports, mutual funds were not aligned with the ₹4,000 Cr (about $419 Mn) valuation sought by Curefoods during its roadshows.

On the financial front, Curefoods’ net loss remained steady at ₹169.9 Cr in FY25 as against ₹172.6 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 27.4% to ₹745.8 Cr compared to ₹585.1 Cr in FY24.

Fibe

Founded in 2015 by Akshay Mehrotra and Ashish Goyal as EarlySalary, Fibe initially offered salary advances and small-ticket personal loans to young working professionals. Since then, it has evolved into a diversified consumer finance platform.

Today, it offers personal loans and purpose-driven financing solutions across sectors such as education, insurance, healthcare, rooftop solar and travel. It claims to operate a merchant network spanning 10,387 touchpoints across India, and claims to have ₹8,603 Cr in assets under management as of March 2026.

It has raised more than $266 Mn from a host of marquee names such as TPG, Norwest Venture Partners, Eight Roads Ventures, Chiratae Ventures, TR Capital, and the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

In June 2026, the lending tech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of up to ₹750 Cr and an OFS component of over 4 Cr shares. It received SEBI’s nod to move ahead with its public offering in September 2026.

On the financial front, Fibe saw its net profit more than double to ₹257.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹113.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue surged 31% to ₹1,584.6 Cr from ₹1,208.9 Cr in FY25.

Garuda Aerospace

Founded in 2015 by Agnishwar Jayaprakash and Rithika Mohann, Garuda Aerospace manufactures over 30 types of drones, while also offering drone-as-a-service (DaaS) solutions. It claims to have trained over 1 Lakh drone pilots, serving more than 100 government agencies along with over 500 enterprises. 

The startup currently operates a fleet of over 400 drones and has a manufacturing capacity of up to 15,000 units annually.

Backed by cricketer MS Dhoni, Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle and Ocgrow Ventures, Garuda Aerospace has raised more than $37.1 Mn in funding to date. It was last pegged at a post-money valuation of $250 Mn during its last fundraise last year. 

The company first signalled its intent to go public in 2023. At the time, Jayaprakash told Inc42 that the company would list on the bourses within two years.

Eventually in April 2026, the Chennai-based dronetech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. While the exact size of the IPO is yet to be determined, the company’s board, in March, approved a proposal to raise up to ₹750 Cr via fresh issue of shares and an undisclosed OFS component.

The startup bagged SEBI’s approval for its IPO in August 2026.

On the financial front, Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹11 Cr in H1 FY26 against an operating revenue of ₹41.2 Cr. 

InCred Holdings

Founded in 2016 by Bhupinder Singh, InCred Group runs three distinct business verticals. InCred Finance handles lending, InCred Capital is focussed on wealth and asset management, while InCred Money specialises in retail bonds and alternative investments.

The company boasts backing from heavyweights like Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), OAKS, Investcorp, Moore Capital, and Elevar Equity, among others.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings in September 2025, InCred Holdings, the parent of InCred Financial Services, sought shareholder approval to raise up to  ₹  1,500 Cr through a fresh issue of shares. 

By November 2025, InCred Holdings filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. The startup received the markets regulator’s nod for its IPO in February 2026.

In May 2026, the company filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a public issue, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,250 Cr and an OFS of up to 9.9 Cr equity shares.

InCred Holdings reported a 5.3% jump in net profit to ₹290 Cr in 9M FY26 from ₹275.5 Cr during the same period last fiscal. Operating revenue also surged 38.6% to ₹1,848.9 Cr from ₹1,333.9 Cr in 9M FY25.

Infra.Market

Founded in 2016 by Souvik Sengupta and Aaditya Sharda, Infra.Market runs a B2B marketplace that helps customers procure construction materials like concrete, steel, pipes, fittings, and chemicals.

The startup has raised over $415 Mn till date from investors such as Tiger Global, Accel, and Nexus Ventures.

In October 2025, Infra.Market confidentially pre-filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI for a nearly ₹5,000 Cr ($563.3 Mn) listing. It received SEBI’s go-ahead in January 2026.

In August 2026, the paint manufacturing giant proposed that it would acquire shares and CCPS of Infra.Market through a swap, involving securities worth around ₹10,545 Cr.

The two companies are also exploring a potential “unification” at a later stage, subject to applicable laws and requisite approvals.

Infra.Market’s net profit dwindled 42% to ₹219.7 Cr in FY25 from ₹378 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, revenue from operations rose 27% to ₹18,472 Cr versus ₹14,530.2 Cr in FY24.

Kuku Technologies

Founded in 2018 by Lal Chand Bisu,Vikas Goyal and Vinod Kumar Meena, Kuku is an audio-centric OTT platform that hosts audiobooks, podcasts, and original shows under Kuku FM in multiple Indian languages. It also operates a vernacular short-video app under Kuku TV brand and a microlearning platform Guru.

The startup claims to have raised more than $156 Mn in funding to date and is backed by marquee names such as Vertex Ventures, Krafton, IFC and Paramark Ventures.

In December 2025, reports first emerged that the OTT soonicorn was looking to list on the bourses. The company is said to have appointed Kotak Mahindra Capital, Axis Bank and Morgan Stanley as bankers to helm its potential IPO. 

In June 2026, Inc42 reported that Kuku filed its DRHP with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr to ₹3,500 Cr (about $261 Mn to $366 Mn) through its IPO. The startup is targeting a valuation of up to ₹15,000 Cr (about $1.8 Bn) for the public listing.

MakeMyTrip

Launched in 2000 by Keyur Joshi, Rajesh Magow, and Deep Kalra, MakeMyTrip is an online travel aggregator (OTA) that operates an end-to-end platform for booking flights, hotels and holiday packages. It also offers ancillary services such as forex cards and travel insurance. 

Over the years, it acquired rivals such as Goibibo and redBus to complement its primary business of air ticketing and hotels. More recently, it also acquired a minority stake in Visa processing platform Atlys and holiday packages business Flamingo Transworld. 

Since its inception, the company claims to have processed over 8.7 Cr transactions for retail consumers and onboarded 77,000 SME and large corporate customers. It was also one of the first Indian startups to list on Nasdaq in 2010.

After Nasdaq, the travel tech major is now eyeing an Indian IPO. In April 2026, reports surfaced that the company appointed Axis Capital, Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan as advisers for the IPO. Subsequently in July 2026, the travel tech major filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route for a $1 Bn OFS-only listing. 

On the financial front, MakeMyTrip reported a nearly 46% YoY decline in its net profit to $51.7 Mn in FY26, while operating revenue rose a mere 6.7% YoY to $1.04 Bn during the fiscal under review.

NoPaperForms

A brainchild of Naveen Goyal and Suraj Sapra, Meritto parent NoPaperForms helps educational institutions and edtech businesses automate student enrollment and fee collection processes. 

Founded in 2017, the startup catered to 1,183 educational institutions, including Manipal University, Shiv Nadar University and PhysicsWallah, in FY26. 

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, Meritto turned into a public entity in May 2025 after its board and shareholders passed a resolution to approve the conversion.

Subsequently, in November 2025, the company filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential route for an IPO, and received approval from the markets regulator to go ahead with its IPO in March 2026.

In September 2026, NoPaperForms filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹375 Cr and an OFS component of up to 3.8 Cr equity shares. 

On the financial front, NoPaperForms reported an operating revenue of ₹115.6 Cr in FY26, up 25.2% from ₹92.3 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, the startup’s profits surged 534% to ₹11.9 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹1.9 Cr in FY25.

OYO (PRISM)

Founded in 2012 by Ritesh Agarwal, OYO, rebranded as PRISM in 2025, is a travel tech major that operates budget hotels, vacation homes, casino hotels, coworking spaces, and corporate stays.

After postponing its IPO plans multiple times, the hospitality giant’s parent entity PRISM secured shareholder nod in December 2025 to raise up to ₹6,650 Cr through a fresh issue of shares. 

Days later, the company confidentially pre-filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI. It eventually received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in June 2026. Right after, the hospitality major filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a ₹6,650 Cr IPO, which will comprise entirely of a fresh issue of shares. 

The company is targeting a valuation of $7 Bn to $8 Bn and has appointed ICICI Securities, Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs, and Citibank to helm the issue.

It once again filed its DRHP via the confidential route for a $600 Mn IPO in 2023, but later withdrew the papers again in May 2024.

On the financial front, PRISM reported a profit of ₹748 Cr in 9M FY26, almost 3X of the ₹245 Cr profit it reported in the full year FY25. Its operating revenue stood at ₹6,941 Cr in 9M FY26, up from ₹6,253 Cr in FY25. 

PhonePe

Founded in 2015 by Sameer Nigam, Rahul Chari, and Burzin Engineer, PhonePe is India’s leading digital payments platform. It regularly accounts for nearly half of all Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions processed in the country. 

Originally focussed on digital payments, the fintech giant has since evolved into a comprehensive financial services provider, offering insurance products, broking services, and more.

PhonePe was acquired by Flipkart in 2016. Six years later, US retail giant and parent Walmart spun it off as a separate entity from Flipkart. The fintech major redomiciled back to India in late 2022, setting the stage for its eventual listing on the Indian exchanges.

In January 2026, the fintech major filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for its IPO, which then consisted solely of an OFS component. 

However, raking a U-Turn, the fintech major, in March 2026, temporarily paused its IPO plans amid geopolitical tensions in West Asia and volatility in the global equity markets. A few months later in September 2026, PhonePe once again revived its listing plans.

Following the re-introduction of a new merchant discount rate (MDR) framework for UPI payments, the Walmart-backed fintech said that it is now targeting a public listing by March 2027. It will now file its updated IPO papers by 2026-end, seeking a valuation of $10 Bn.

Financially, PhonePe’s net loss widened by 62% to ₹2,792 Cr in FY26 as against ₹1,727.4 Cr reported in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 11.5% to ₹7,920.5 Cr from ₹7,105 Cr in FY25.

PlaySimple Games

Founded in 2014 by Siddharth Jain, Siddhanth Jain, Preeti Reddy, and Suraj Nalin, PlaySimple Games is a casual mobile gaming studio. It operates a portfolio of 30 live mobile games across five categories – search, crossword, anagram, other word games, and non-word puzzles.

It claims to have a presence in more than 110 countries. The startup was acquired by Swedish gaming company MTG for more than $360 Mn in 2021. Prior to the acquisition, PlaySimple raised $4.5 Mn in funding from the likes of Elevation Capital and Chiratae Ventures.

In April 2026, PlaySimple filed its DRHP with SEBI for a public issue which will comprise solely an OFS component of ₹3,150 Cr. MTGx Gaming Holding AB will be the lone seller during the listing. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in August 2026.

If listed, PlaySimple will become the second gaming company to go public in India, after Nazara Technologies.

On the financial front, PlaySimple reported an operating revenue of ₹2,259.8 Cr in CY2025, up 20% YoY. However, net profit declined 31% YoY to ₹359 Cr, largely due to a 54% surge in advertising and sales commission costs.

Razorpay

Founded in 2014 by IIT-Roorkee alumni Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar, Razorpay has evolved from a simple payment gateway to an omnichannel fintech giant for payments, banking, SME payroll, lending, insurance, and more.

It claims to process an annualised total payment volume (TPV) exceeding $180 Bn and caters to a majority of India’s unicorns. 

Kicking off its IPO plans, the company reverse flipped back to India in May 2025 by merging its US-based entity with its Indian arm Razorpay Software Pvt Ltd. In June 2026, the unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route. The startup is said to be looking to raise anywhere between $500 Mn to $700 Mn at a valuation of $5 Bn to $6 Bn, lower than its last private valuation of $7.5 Bn. 

Razorpay has so far raised nearly $740 Mn from heavyweights such as Y Combinator, Tiger Global, Peak XV Partners, Lone Pine Capital, Alkeon Capital, and GIC.

The startup’s net profit skyrocketed 365% to ₹33.5 Cr in FY24 from ₹7.2 Cr in the year-ago period, even as operating revenue shot up a mere 9% to ₹2,475 Cr from ₹2,283 Cr in FY23.

Razorpay claimed that it slipped into the red in FY25 due to an ESOP expense of ₹1,209 Cr and tax payments linked to its reverse flip to India. Meanwhile, operating revenue is said to have surged 65% YoY to ₹3,783 Cr in FY25.

StockGro

On the financial front, the startup closed FY26 with a net profit of ₹113 Cr, up 226.6% from ₹34.6 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, revenue from operations nearly doubled to ₹226.1 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹113.3 Cr in FY25.

Table Space

On the financial front, Zepto’s net loss widened 26% to ₹5,905.2 Cr in FY26 as against ₹4,699.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue more than doubled to ₹22,623.6 Cr during the year under review from ₹11,109.9 Cr in FY25.
