item.title: India Can Build Rockets, But Can Its VCs Fund The Next One?
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: On July 18, 2026, Skyroot Aerospace achieved a historic milestone when its Vikram-1 rocket successfully placed satellites into orbit, becoming…
item.content:encoded:
On July 18, 2026, Skyroot Aerospace achieved a historic milestone when its Vikram-1 rocket successfully placed satellites into orbit, becoming the first privately developed Indian rocket to accomplish an orbital launch.

For a country whose space programme was historically dominated by ISRO, it was a powerful demonstration of what Indian entrepreneurs could achieve in advanced technology.

Three months later, Ashlee Vance — the American journalist best known for his bestselling biography of Elon Musk and reporting on the global space industry — turned his attention to India’s technological ambitions.

His question was less about the capabilities of Indian engineers than the willingness of Indian investors to back them. He asked: 

“Why are Indian VCs so afraid to take risk and make money?”

The October 22 post accompanied Vance’s Core Memory feature exploring India’s emerging hardware economy.

After three weeks meeting 15 Indian companies, Vance appeared impressed by the technological ambitions of their founders but far less enthusiastic about the state of the country’s venture capital ecosystem. He subsequently doubled down, claiming he had rarely encountered a market where VCs had a worse reputation among founders.

What followed was an unusually candid debate.

Founders complained about investors demanding commercial traction before technologies had been validated, prolonged diligence processes and excessive dependence on founder pedigree.

Investors pushed back, highlighting India’s growing list of deeptech successes, the increasing availability of specialist capital and the structural challenges of financing scientific innovation.

But the timing makes this debate far more consequential than another disagreement on X.

As AI threatens to automate parts of the software-services industry that helped establish India as a global technology powerhouse, the country’s ability to create and own foundational technologies is becoming increasingly important.

India has demonstrated that its entrepreneurs can build complex technologies. The more difficult question is whether venture capital and private equity can repeatedly back such breakthroughs.

Indian Founders Aren’t Just Questioning Capital, They’re Questioning The VCs

One of the strongest responses came from Akash Kulgod, founder of Dognosis, which is developing canine-assisted cancer detection technology.

In a detailed post, Kulgod compared his experience interacting with approximately 80 investors, around 65% of whom were based in the US. His criticism ran deeper than simply stating that Indian VCs rejected his startup.

He said US investors typically made relatively quick decisions, rejecting the opportunity when they lacked conviction in the technology or founding team.

Some Indian investors, he alleged, extended discussions over repeated meetings and visits, only to demand commercial traction or stop responding. For a company developing medical technology, any delays in the development cycle hurt.

Clinical validation, technical testing and regulatory approvals can require years before meaningful commercial revenue becomes possible.

An investor demanding revenue before the technology is proven may effectively eliminate the opportunity instead of properly evaluating the technology.

Kulgod also questioned whether some investors possessed the technical understanding needed to assess unfamiliar scientific problems.

Other founders raised concerns about investor dependence on IIT or IIM credentials, professional networks and the reputations of existing backers when evaluating early-stage startups.

These are undoubtedly individual accounts, not evidence that such practices are universal across Indian VC firms. But they expose an uncomfortable question.

If investors require commercial traction, institutional validation and another investor’s conviction before writing a cheque, how much technological risk are they actually underwriting?

There is an important difference between financing a technology after it works and financing the experiment that determines whether it can work.

Deeptech needs both. And as the experience of several founders in India shows, the latter remains one of the most difficult investment decisions.

The Numbers Show A Funding Surge, But Are More Founders Benefiting?

According to Inc42 DataLabs, Indian deeptech startups raised approximately $500 Mn across 87 deals in 2025.

The sector emerged as one of the most active by deal count, but its funding remained substantially below fintech’s $2.5 Bn, enterprise tech’s $1.8 Bn and ecommerce’s $1.7 Bn.

The latest quarterly figures, however, suggest that investor preferences are changing.

In Q3 2026, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 funding deals, compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in the year-ago quarter.

Funding surged 176% YoY, dramatically outpacing the broader startup ecosystem’s 5% growth.

Deeptech funding nearly tripled, but the number of funded deals actually declined.

Pixxel’s $100 Mn funding round alone accounted for approximately one-third of the deeptech capital deployed during the quarter.

Bengaluru captured around 65% of the sector’s funding.

At the broader ecosystem level, investors also wrote larger seed cheques to fewer companies. Early stage funding fell 18% YoY to $164 Mn across 93 deals, even as the median cheque size increased 20% to $1.2 Mn.

The contrast with the first half of 2026 is instructive.

According to Inc42’s H1 2026 funding report, advanced hardware and technology startups raised $365 Mn across a record 66 deals, reflecting an 18% rise in funding and a 53% jump in deal volume.

That suggests improving breadth of investment during the first half, followed by greater concentration in the third quarter.

There’s no trend to explore here, but this disparity demonstrates why headline funding growth is an insufficient measure of access to capital. Larger investments are increasingly flowing towards a smaller pool of technically validated companies.

So the deeper question is whether more first-time founders pursuing unproven technologies are securing their first institutional cheques, which strikes at the heart of what Vance was saying. 

Are India’s VCs Backing Convenience Over Breakthroughs?

A separate debate over India’s startup funding priorities had already exposed a fundamental divide between founders and investors over where venture capital should flow.

In an October 17 post on X, Neosapien founder Dhananjay Yadav questioned why consumer-service startups burning substantial amounts of capital could attract large investments, while deeptech companies generating higher revenues with lower cash burn struggled to raise even a fraction of that money.

Responding to Yadav, Untitled Ventures’ Anmol Maini made a provocative claim that much of deeptech could eventually prove to be a “grift”, arguing that quick commerce and on-demand services might contribute more to the economy.

Blume Ventures partner Arpit Agarwal offered an explanation rooted in investment economics.

Investment capital, he argued, gravitates towards opportunities offering lower perceived risk or disproportionately higher returns. 

The distinction to note here is that the economic importance of a technology and its attractiveness as a venture investment are not necessarily the same thing.

This is consistent with concerns Agarwal had raised in an earlier interview with Inc42, where he explained why capital-intensive original equipment manufacturing (OEM) businesses are often poorly suited to conventional early-stage VC financing.

Pixxel founder Awais Ahmed, however, challenged the notion that consumer internet and deeptech should be competing for relevance and the same pie of venture capital.

In a detailed post, Ahmed argued that they represent different layers of the same technological economy.

A ten-minute grocery delivery depends on decades of breakthroughs in semiconductors, GPS, lithium-ion batteries, cellular networks and computing — technologies developed long before their commercial applications became apparent.

Consumer businesses make technology accessible at scale. Deeptech expands what technology can achieve.

Ahmed acknowledged that successful internet companies create wealth that can eventually be reinvested into deeptech. But foundational technologies cannot simply be treated as investments to pursue once quicker commercial opportunities have been exhausted.

Developing competitive capabilities in semiconductors, aerospace, advanced materials or energy requires years of research, specialised talent, experimentation and industrial infrastructure.

And therein lies India’s venture capital allocation dilemma.

The country has spent the past decade building a thriving consumer internet economy. But its ambition to emerge as a global technology powerhouse will require investing in foundational technologies long before their commercial returns become predictable.

The Criticism Ignores How Far India Has Come

Unacademy cofounder Gaurav Munjal was among the prominent voices challenging Vance. In a response on X, Munjal described the assessment as dated and rage-baiting.

He pointed to Astrobase, Airbound and Sarvam AI as examples of ambitious companies successfully raising capital, while highlighting the outcomes achieved by Groww, Eternal and Meesho.

His broader argument was that India’s VC ecosystem had improved dramatically, and that fintech and digital commerce remained important opportunities given the size of the domestic market.

Ather Energy attracted early support from IIT Madras-linked programmes, the Flipkart founders, Tiger Global and Hero MotoCorp before eventually becoming a listed company.

Skyroot has achieved orbital launch capability. Agnikul has demonstrated indigenous launch technology. Pixxel is developing hyperspectral satellites, while Airbound is attempting to commercialise autonomous aircraft.

Munjal’s point was that these achievements challenge the idea that India lacks investors willing to finance complex technologies.

Nevertheless, several high-profile deeptech startups have relied significantly on overseas capital. Airbound’s $37 Mn Series A, for instance, was led by US-based Greenoaks.

An Indian startup’s ability to attract international investors is a sign of some success for the company, but it does not necessarily establish that domestic investors are equally willing to finance such technologies.

Still, Munjal’s argument gains weight from his own next move.

Along with Unacademy cofounder Roman Saini, he is raising a ₹700 Cr fund called Longshot Capital, targeting AI, manufacturing, robotics, spacetech and defence.

It represents a growing pattern: founders who created wealth and operating expertise through India’s first startup generation are increasingly attempting to finance its next.

Indian VCs Have Avoided Real Venture Risk, But That Is Changing

Antler India partner Nitin Sharma offered one of the more balanced assessments.

In a detailed October 24 post, Sharma acknowledged that India’s venture ecosystem had historically failed to generate consistent venture-scale returns partly because investors avoided genuine venture risk.

But he argued that the situation had begun changing.

Sharma identified two categories of founders increasingly receiving backing: the first being experienced technologists and academics, and the second category covering young, unconventional self-taught entrepreneurs.

Sharma said Antler had acted as the first institutional believer in 10 deeptech ventures since 2022.

He highlighted Antler’s investments in companies such as InspeCity, Aspera Aerospace, Green Aero Propulsion, Meine Electric, Mandrake Bio and Armory Shield.

His argument went beyond showing that VCs were willing to invest before revenue. Historically, he explained, early-stage investors were reluctant to back complex technologies partly because they could not identify who would finance those companies in subsequent rounds.

That problem is beginning to ease as specialist funds and larger deeptech investors emerge.

But Sharma acknowledged that India still needs more investors willing to write larger first cheques for ambitious technological bets.

He also identified another serious challenge: demand.

Indian deeptech startups, he argued, struggle to secure paid pilots and procurement opportunities from domestic corporations, particularly outside defence and space.

If Indian companies refuse to become early customers, startups must finance not only technological development but also the prolonged process of creating a commercial market.

India’s investor appetite may be improving. But the institutional and structural environment around deeptech financing and commercialisation must improve with it.

What Established VCs Have Actually Invested

While newer specialist funds are attracting attention, established Indian VC firms have also been investing in deeptech for years.

TC Meenakshisundaram (TCM), cofounder and vice-chairman of Chiratae Ventures, offered a historical perspective in an X thread responding to Vance.

He acknowledged that until 2020, many Indian VCs — including Indian arms of Silicon Valley funds — were reluctant to back hardware and deeptech startups. Concerns over global competitiveness, licensing and certification requirements, the availability of follow-on capital and long investment holding periods have all contributed to this reluctance. 

But he argued that the situation had since changed, highlighting companies such as Quanfluence, TakeMe2Space, Cavli Wireless and Metadome.

Chiratae’s investment record supports that counterargument.

Founded in 2006 by Sudhir Sethi and TCM, the firm reports having deployed more than $300 Mn across over 60 deeptech companies spanning AI, climate technology, healthcare, robotics, spacetech and advanced manufacturing.

In December 2025, it launched its Sonic DeepTech programme to accelerate seed-to-Series A decisions, offering cheques of up to $2 Mn.

By May 2026, Chiratae had announced commitments of up to $10 Mn across five startups selected through the programme.

And Chiratae is hardly alone.

This is a counterpoint to the suggestion that Indian VCs have uniformly avoided advanced technologies. But the criticism is also valid, and therefore it raises the question of how deeptech investment should be measured.

The category includes everything from software-led AI applications to capital-intensive aerospace, advanced manufacturing and medical technologies, each carrying different levels of scientific uncertainty and commercial risk.

The more meaningful measure is not simply how many deeptech companies a fund has backed. It is how early the fund entered, what technical risks it financed and whether it supported those companies through subsequent development cycles.

The Problem Goes Beyond The First Cheque

Founders frequently identify seed funding as their biggest obstacle. Some deeptech investors believe the more serious capital shortage appears later.

Speciale Invest, for instance, outlined plans for a ₹1,400 Cr growth-stage fund targeting companies that have demonstrated technical capabilities but need larger amounts of capital for manufacturing and commercial expansion.

A company like Skyroot, which is making rockets, requires funding for design, testing and initial launches. But technological success is only the beginning of the journey towards reliable commercial operations.

Similarly, a semiconductor company may develop a functioning chip but still need substantial capital for fabrication, qualification and customer adoption.

Deeptech businesses require a continuous financing pipeline.

The problem for India is the insufficient seed capital for highly speculative technologies and inadequate growth capital for technically validated companies. Both gaps exist simultaneously.

When the next investor is missing, even the first investor becomes more reluctant to take the risk.

The Capital Powering India’s VCs

Siana Capital’s Siddharth Shah raised another structural issue in his response to the debate.

He argued that India’s venture capital ecosystem is constrained by the expectations of limited partners — the investors financing venture funds.

Deeptech companies can require 10–15 years to achieve meaningful commercial maturity. Yet VC funds often operate within shorter investment and distribution timelines.

One problem is LPs seeking distributions while portfolio companies were still working towards critical technical or commercial milestones.

He also highlighted weak secondary liquidity, difficult exits and the limited availability of long-duration domestic institutional capital.

US-based investor Anu Hariharan raised related concerns about taxation, currency exposure, operational complexity and limited M&A opportunities.

The H1 2026 Inc42 funding report offers another perspective.

While 64% of surveyed institutional investors said they expected to increase their venture capital allocations, respondents also identified geopolitical uncertainty and constrained global liquidity as major risks.

Investor expectations around exits have also shifted. Strategic acquisitions and secondary transactions are increasingly important alternatives to IPOs, particularly for companies unlikely to reach public-market scale quickly.

The problem is that risk appetite is shaped by the economics of the entire investment value chain.

LPs want returns and liquidity. VCs need successful exits to raise their next funds. Corporate customers want proven products. Founders need financing to prove those products work.

Each participant may be making a rational individual decision. But collectively, those decisions can produce a system in which everyone expects somebody else to absorb the earliest uncertainty.

That does not absolve VCs of responsibility for poor diligence or insufficient conviction.

Changing India’s deeptech investment culture will require more than persuading fund managers to be courageous.

Deeptech Funds Changing The Capital Landscape

There is, however, evidence that the supply of dedicated capital is growing.

In the past year alone, India has seen a wave of new funds and investment vehicles targeting AI, spacetech, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, energy and industrial technologies.

Aakrit Vaish, the former Haptik CEO, and Pratyush Choudhury launched AI-focused VC firm Activate in December 2025.

By September 2026, Activate had closed its investment platform at $105 Mn, comprising an $85 Mn early-stage fund and $20 Mn deployed through growth investment vehicles.

Its portfolio includes investments in Sarvam AI, ElevenLabs and Wispr Flow, alongside early-stage bets that have not been publicly disclosed.

The fund’s investor base includes founders, AI researchers, global VC partners and family offices — a different pool of capital from the institutions that traditionally dominated Indian startup financing.

Meanwhile, Transition VC launched a ₹1,500 Cr second fund in July, targeting energy transition, advanced manufacturing and industrial deeptech businesses.

Unlike many conventional seed funds, Transition VC plans to write $2 Mn-$5 Mn cheques into engineering-led startups demonstrating technical feasibility and early commercial traction.

The investment strategies differ, but the pattern is becoming more visible.

The emergence of these funds suggests that India’s financing ecosystem is becoming more specialised. But their mandates also demonstrate that deeptech capital is not interchangeable.

Longshot and AUM are targeting early-stage opportunities. Piper Serica and Speciale’s proposed growth fund focus on companies further along their development journeys. Transition VC targets engineering-led businesses that have already established technical feasibility.

YourNest’s continuation fund addresses another problem: providing additional time and liquidity for existing portfolio companies rather than financing entirely new startups.

More capital is entering deeptech. The unanswered question is whether these different sources of funding will connect to create an uninterrupted financing pipeline from research to commercial scale.

Government Support Is Influencing Investor Conviction, But Execution Matters

The government is also attempting to address the patient-capital shortage. And government policy is also beginning to shape private investment decisions.

Its ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation scheme is designed to support high-risk, research-intensive technologies.

In October, the government approved 19 second-level fund managers with commitments totalling ₹7,131 Cr.

That is a significant development, although the overall scheme outlay should not be confused with capital already deployed to startups.

According to Inc42’s H1 2026 investor survey, 61% of respondents said the India Semiconductor Mission had influenced their investment thesis for deeptech and hardware, while 66% said the IndiaAI Mission had influenced their AI investment thesis.

But this policy support does not automatically translate into greater appetite for every type of frontier technology.

Inc42’s Q3 2026 survey of more than 85 institutional investors found that 39% expected vertical AI applications to capture the most value over the next five years, compared with 23% favouring AI hardware and semiconductors and 14% backing sovereign foundation models.

Investors are interested in foundational technologies, but their expectations of where AI value will accrue remain weighted towards applications. These are survey preferences, not actual deal allocations, and the reality of the investments of these funds will differ from their responses. 

Nevertheless, they suggest that even within a booming technology category, investors remain selective about where value is most likely to accrue.

The RDI programme itself has faced questions over governance.

In our Q3 survey, 52% of respondents considered existing disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate but said transparency remained limited. A quarter of the respondents (25%) called for independent oversight.

The government’s role will therefore need to extend beyond announcing larger financing schemes.

Transparent allocation, research commercialisation, industrial procurement and access to testing infrastructure will influence whether policy support ultimately produces sustainable companies.

India’s spacetech reforms offer one example of what coordinated support can achieve.

Skyroot and Agnikul’s technological progress cannot be separated from the policy changes and institutional infrastructure that enabled private participation in the country’s space economy.

The next challenge is to build similarly effective pathways across semiconductors, advanced materials, medical technologies, energy and industrial automation.

It is no longer whether India can produce another Ather, Skyroot or Pixxel.

It is whether an unknown scientist or engineer with a genuinely ambitious idea can access the capital, research infrastructure, industrial customers and follow-on investment needed to attempt something equally difficult.

Not every rocket will reach orbit. Not every chip will work. Not every scientific breakthrough will become a commercially viable company.

But financing those uncertain attempts is precisely what allows an innovation ecosystem to produce breakthroughs at scale.

India has proved that its founders can build rockets. Now it must prove that its capital ecosystem can finance the next hundred, including the ones that never leave the launchpad.

item.content:encoded:
For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to an adult. Among the clearest signs of evolution and maturity of this ecosystem is the growing number of startups eyeing a public listing now.

For Indian companies, achieving a public listing has for long symbolised operational progression, transparency, and long-term viability. For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation.

Currently, a handful of startups, including the likes of Razorpay, PRISM, PhonePe, among others, are in various stages of their IPO journey. Meanwhile, over 70 Indian new-age tech companies have already crossed the milestone and are now listed on the bourses.

The list also includes Indian companies like MakeMyTrip and Freshworks, which are listed on Nasdaq in the US.

India’s startup IPO wave reached its peak in 2025, surpassing the previous year’s momentum.

While 18 startups listed in 2025, 17 startups have already reached that milestone in 2026. With companies like Cult.fit, OYO, others, eyeing to tap the public markets this year, the list is only expected to grow further this year.

17 new-age companies — Tonbo Imaging, Zetwerk, AceVector, Moneyview, Rentomojo, ESDS, Purple Style Labs, Turtlemint, Klassroom, Shiprocket, LEAP India, Kissht, Aye Finance, Fractal Analytics, Amagi, Shadowfax and SEDEMAC — have made their public market debut in 2026.

As of now, the total market capitalisation of the listed companies stands at over $167 Bn.

To consolidate all the information about listed startups, Inc42 has launched the Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker. From the movement in the shares of the companies since their listing to the financial performance of these companies, the tracker is your one-stop resource to know everything you need about the listed tech companies.

Read our methodology here. 

Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride

Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. 

While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges.

While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. Over 60 of the new-age tech companies are currently profitable.

In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. 

It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s purview are about a decade old. 

From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra’s IPO materialised within four years of its operations.  

Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal.

Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr

Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom

The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem.

The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups.

While fintech and ecommerce house 14 names each, 13 enterprise tech startups have listed on the bourses so far. 

The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of Tonbo Imaging, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts.

Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups

While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 27 listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru’s ninetineen and Mumbai’s fifteen. 

While fifteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube. 

Delhi NCR contributes $96 Bn in the cumulative $178 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies.

item.title: eMudhra Has Quit TLS. The Accountability Questions Haven’t
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: On October 27, Google removed eMudhra’s root certificate called emSign ECC Root CA – G3. Any website still relying on…
item.content:encoded:
On October 27, Google removed eMudhra’s root certificate called emSign ECC Root CA – G3. Any website still relying on it began showing Chrome users a full-page security warning.

This action follows a series of events that unfolded in mid-October with Bengaluru-based eMudhra, India’s largest licensed certifying authority, at the centre of it all. 

A researcher had shown that the private keys of eight certificate authorities under eMudhra’s global hierarchy were so weak that anyone could work them out. One of them was the number 4.

What followed was swift action, at least outside India. All major browser makers blocked the certificates within hours. Software maintainers shipped emergency patches and eMudhra revoked the certificates. 

Within five days of the vulnerability being reported, eMudhra’s board decided to exit the global TLS certificate business altogether.

However, in India, the response to this security incident has been noticeably slower. 

The IT ministry (MeitY) has formed a special team to investigate and CERT-In issued an advisory four days after the initial report of the vulnerability. 

While eMudhra has walked away from a business that it says contributes 1% of its revenue, the question is who holds a certificate authority accountable in India? What rules may have been broken by eMudhra in the process of this still-developing situation, and what could the penalties be? 

How The Browsers Shut The Door

The trouble began well before October. The eight keys were created at a single key ceremony, the formal process in which a certificate authority generates its keys, on April 30, 2025. Industry rules require such ceremonies to follow a written script, to be watched by a qualified auditor or recorded on video, and to be signed off in an auditor’s report.

eMudhra claims a flaw in its script created a second, weak set of keys, which were used by mistake because their labels looked similar. Each key should have been about 116 digits long; all eight were below 256. The flaw went undetected for about 18 months, across two audit cycles. “I don’t know. We went through two external audit cycles,” said Kaushik Srinivasan, cofounder, eMudhra, calling it “a one-off, a bad day.” An auditor’s report is due in two to three weeks.

Once a researcher flagged the weak keys on October 17, the response from browser makers was immediate.

Google was swift on its feet by reacting in an hour and 40 minutes later after it received the researcher’s report on October 17. Google’s Chrome had blocked the six website-securing certificates through CRLSet, a blocklist it pushes to browsers without needing an update or restart.

Mozilla moved almost as fast. It blocked the certificates in Mozilla Firefox within hours of receiving the report. It also released browser updates and is updating its wider certificate store to protect other applications. Apple followed on October 19 with patches for Safari and Microsoft on October 20 for Edge and legacy versions of its browsers. 

These companies — some of the biggest tech companies in the world — then went a step further. So on October 20, Mozilla removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 root from its trusted list, and Chrome removed it from the Chrome Root Store, effective October 27. It is also said at the time that it is investigating whether eMudhra’s remaining roots should stay in Chrome. 

Removing eMudhra’s root access is a heavier step than blocking a certificate. It means that a user’s operating system, web browser, or software application no longer automatically trusts or accepts digital certificates issued by that affected Certificate Authority (CA) or tied to that specific root key. 

There was one piece of reassurance. Chrome said no website certificate from the six intermediates had appeared in public Certificate Transparency logs before its block, so none could have been used against Chrome or other software that requires such logging.

Where TLS Fits In eMudhra’s Business

eMudhra was founded in 2008 and listed on the BSE and NSE in 2022. Among its customers, Government and defence account for 30% of its revenue, banking and financial services for 25%, and other enterprises for 45%. It operates mainly in two lines of business: enterprise software and trust services.

Enterprise software is now the core of the business. It sells platforms like emSigner, for digital document signing; SecurePass, for identity and access management; CertiNext, which helps organisations track and renew their certificates.

Trust services is the certificate business. eMudhra issues digital signature certificates, which are electronic identities used to legally sign digital documents, verify the signer’s identity, and file online forms. In India, the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) regulates and permits CAs like eMudhra to issue digital signature certificates.  

Users could buy a digital signature certificate either for themselves or for an established organisation on eMudhra Digital website. The company said it handled digital signatures for India’s income tax, GST, customs and company law filings. 

Additionally, eMudhra also offers electronic signature or eSign services. It is an Aadhaar-based electronic signature service that allows individuals and businesses to sign documents remotely without physical paperwork. In 2015, CCA empanelled eMudhra as an authorised eSign service provider.  

Outside India, eMudhra issues digital signature certificates to individuals and organisations under its own emSign root brand, and is licensed or approved as a provider by governments including Kenya, UAE, and Mauritius. It is accredited by the independent audit and assurance program called WebTrust. 

eMudhra’s trust services also include SSL/TLS certificates, the digital credentials that secure websites, sold under the same emSign brand. A website owner buys a certificate from a certificate authority (CA) such as eMudhra. When someone visits the site, their browser checks whether the certificate comes from a CA it trusts. If it does, the browser encrypts the connection and shows the padlock; if not, it warns the visitor away.

That trust is decided by browser makers such as Google, Apple, Mozilla and Microsoft, which keep their own lists of approved CAs and set the rules those CAs must follow through the CA/Browser Forum — a voluntary industry consortium of CAs and web browser vendors.

According to the company, the customers for this service included a university federation in the US, and a few government departments and private sector companies outside the US. 

Following the distrust action, On October 22, eMudhra announced that it has decided to wind up this SSL/TLS certificate business, withdrawing not just the affected G3 root, but also G1 root. “The impact has been quite severe over the last 24-48 hours. Given the risk to the rest of the business and our obligations as a publicly listed company, the board felt it was prudent to withdraw from this business,” said Srinivasan.

The company also cited rising compliance costs, declining returns and limited revenue contribution as the reason behind the move. The segment accounts for around 1% of this publicly listed company’s global revenue. The company reported revenues of ₹701.6 Cr in FY26.

The segment’s future commercial prospects also triggered the closure. With Let’s Encrypt offering free TLS certificates and Cloudflare planning to do the same, Srinivasan said the commercial return from the business looks limited, particularly as browser guidelines move towards 90-day certificates.

MeitY has drawn the line in its official statement on the matter that the incident concerns eMudhra’s internationally audited website and software certificates, and that its Indian DSC and eSign services remain unaffected.

The Question Of Accountability

That distinction matters for accountability. As a licensed certifying authority, under the IT Act, the company is obliged to use secure procedures, disclose facts that may affect its reliability. Additionally, Information Technology (Certifying Authorities) Rules, 2000, requires the certifying authority’s operations to be audited every year, with each audit report sent to the CCA within four weeks. IFF argues these duties still reach the emSign business, because eMudhra’s own staff ran the failed ceremony. 

CERT-In’s role raises its own questions. Its 2022 Directions require companies to report any of 15 listed types of cyber incidents, including the compromise of critical systems or information, within six hours of noticing them. CERT-In’s advisory says eMudhra reported the compromise, but not when. 

Finally, the data protection law. The DPDP Act’s security safeguards and breach-notification duties take effect only on May 13, 2027, and they apply to personal data.

eMudhra says no customer data was accessed. If personal data had been breached, the DPDP Act, once in force in May 2027, would require the company to inform affected users and the Data Protection Board without delay and file a detailed report with the Board within 72 hours. Failing to report a breach can draw a penalty of up to ₹200 Cr, and failing to maintain reasonable security safeguards up to ₹250 Cr, explained Akshayy S Nanda, Partner, Saraf & Partners.

“A weak or vulnerable key would not, by itself, establish that a personal-data breach occurred. However, it could allow malicious actors to create web pages or sites that appear legitimate and pass security checks,” said Nikhil Jhanji, principal product manager at IDfy, which runs the DPDP compliance platform Privy. Jhanji added that organisations using eMudhra’s services should review their vendor-risk practices, and that the incident should prompt a review of other vendors handling personal data. 

So far, the only penalty eMudhra has faced is the one the browsers imposed. Indian law offers several more, but most come with a catch. The heaviest Indian lever, licence revocation, would hit the DSC business that did not fail, rather than the TLS business that did. That mismatch is the core of the governance gap.

“As far as the IT Act is concerned, the penalties are fairly dated. Compared to the kind of damage and losses people suffer, they don’t necessarily reflect the risks and threats that the ecosystem faces today and are not proportionate to the level of risk exposure in the market, and I would say they are very modest,” said Shreya Suri, Partner at law firm CMS INDUSLAW. 

“CERT-In is a reporting and investigative agency, and in cases of non-compliance, it can be called upon to take action. As far as penalties go, a licence suspension or revocation would be the most disruptive consequence for a business and its operations, and it would send a strong message,” she added.

Will eMudhra Be Investigated?

The magnitude of the incident complicates the picture too, even though eMudhra has consistently tried to play it down. 

While no attack using the keys has been reported, the keys were effectively public for about 18 months, around 30,000 certificates were affected for a single US client, and software makers shipped emergency fixes. All of this suggests the situation is a lot more serious than what eMudhra has publicly stated. 

Even the IT Ministry (MeitY) calls the Indian impact limited, despite the fact that many key government websites, including the Aadhaar issuer UIDAI and the income tax filing portal, use digital certificates or other technology from eMudhra. 

There’s also a matter that came up in the early days of the vulnerability being disclosed and reported.  Devices that cannot be updated may keep trusting the bad certificates for longer and this leaves a whole chunk of web-connected devices vulnerable to attacks.

Government departments do initiate investigations in such matters involving cybersecurity issues and lapses, but they tend to focus more on damage control than on accountability for what has already happened, said CMS INDUSLAW’s Suri. 

Investigations identify vulnerabilities and gaps in systems, determine how they can be mitigated, and establish measures to keep systems up to date. Organisations may also conduct annual audits. These are all remedial actions aimed at preventing a recurrence. 

“That forward-looking approach is better than nothing, but there is still a lack of accountability for what has already happened. As things stand, I don’t think there is any quantifiable accountability in terms of the consequences faced by those responsible,” she added.

The Cost For India

India has been on the receiving end of browser enforcement before. In 2014, after the National Informatics Centre misissued certificates for Google domains, Google restricted the India CCA root to a handful of Indian domains such as gov.in and nic.in.

The bill for eMudhra is a small revenue line and a large reputational one. The bill for India may last longer.

eMudhra was a major Indian root certificate authority trusted by browsers worldwide. Once its exit is complete, Indian websites may have to depend largely on foreign certificate authorities for the padlock in the address bar. 

“When news like this comes out about a company that supports our PKI infrastructure, it raises concerns about both the company’s reputation and the country’s reputation… People may start to question whether PKI infrastructure provided by Indian companies can be trusted,” said Abhijeet Zilpelwar, cofounder and CTO of pi-labs.

The assurance that India’s own DSC and eSign systems are unaffected also rests, for now, largely on eMudhra’s claims and accounts. 

The company has told Mozilla and other browsers it will re-verify every key ceremony it has run. Until someone independently checks that work, Indian users have only the company’s word and MeitY’s preliminary view. But what we have seen is a complete breakdown of the trust in a company whose entire business hinges on trust. Will eMudhra end up paying a bigger price for this mistake than it has so far? 

[Edited by Nikhil Subramaniam]

item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil

item.content:encoded:
Delhi NCR-based D2C skincare brand Numour is in talks to raise nearly $3.1 Mn (about ₹30 Cr) in a funding round led by Sharrp Ventures, sources told Inc42.

The brand, which combines skincare formulations with beauty devices, is currently backed by Indian Silicon Valley Capital.

Questions sent to Numour and Sharrp Ventures did not elicit a response till the time of publication. 

Founded in 2025 by Divya Jain, Numour operates through Nuvanza Venture. Besides its own website, the brand says it sells through ecommerce platforms Amazon, Nykaa, Flipkart, and Myntra, and quick commerce platform Blinkit. It also has an offline presence through Broadway stores.

Its product portfolio includes sunscreens, dual-phase serums, collagen-based skincare products, LED-equipped jars, sonic massagers, and facial devices. Some products incorporate red or blue LEDs, while others feature sonic massage technology.

Numour says its product development centres on three areas: active ingredients, skin barrier care, and delivery technology. The brand claims its formulations combine clinically validated ingredients with delivery systems designed to carry active ingredients beyond the skin’s surface barrier.
It positions itself at the intersection of skincare and consumer technology.
Sharrp Ventures is the investment office of the Harsh Mariwala family. Its investments span businesses across categories such as beauty and personal care, consumer technology, health and wellness, food and beverages, and lifestyle.

In July, it led ₹100 Cr funding round of beauty and personal care contract manufacturer Naturis Cosmetics.

Numour’s fundraising talks come amid investments in skincare brands. In May, CHOSEN raised $5 Mn in a Series A round led by Fireside Ventures, with participation from L’Oreal’s venture capital arm BOLD and Alkemi Growth Capital. The brand earmarked the capital for strengthening R&D, expanding its product pipeline, and scaling its team and centre of excellence.

At the heart of these investments is India’s growing D2C market, which is projected to grow from $65 Bn in 2026 to $310 Bn by 2031, at a CAGR of around 37%.

item.title: Can D-Propulse Help India Reduce Its Dependence On Foreign Missile Engine Technology?
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: For nearly four decades, India has chased the dream of building its own jet engine, but the breakthrough remains elusive.…
item.content:encoded:
For nearly four decades, India has chased the dream of building its own jet engine, but the breakthrough remains elusive. The result? Continued dependence on foreign technology, expensive imports, external vendors and lengthy overseas testing.

D-Propulse is attempting to address one part of this challenge through a new propulsion technology that promises lighter, more efficient engines for high-speed applications. 

Founded in 2025 by defence analyst Saurav Jha and former DRDO scientist Dr V Ramanujachari, D-Propulse is developing rotating detonation engines (RDEs) for high-speed drones and missiles. Unlike conventional engines that burn fuel through a steady flame, RDEs use supersonic detonation waves to generate thrust, potentially improving fuel efficiency while reducing engine size and complexity.

Jha, who founded Delhi Defence Review, identified gaps in India’s indigenous propulsion capabilities through his work on military and strategic affairs. Ramanujachari, who previously led DRDO’s scramjet engine programme and contributed to the Akash missile’s propulsion system, had spent several years researching RDE technology at IIT Madras. Together, they saw an opportunity to translate that research into commercially viable propulsion systems. 

An Indian Jet Engine For The World

Unlike conventional jet engines that burn fuel through a steady flame, D-Propulse’s rotating detonation engines (RDEs) use supersonic combustion waves to generate thrust.

Here’s how it works: A spark ignites a mixture of fuel and air, creating a shockwave that travels around a ring-shaped combustion chamber thousands of times a second. As it moves, the wave continuously compresses and ignites fresh fuel and air, producing high-pressure gases that are expelled to generate thrust.

This process could make RDEs more fuel-efficient, compact and mechanically simpler than conventional engines, potentially making them suitable for high-speed missiles and drones. 

According to Jha, their engine is “15-25% thermally more efficient than an air-breathing jet engine”. He said the RDE requires simpler hardware, fewer moving parts compared with conventional gas turbines and can be produced at scale.

In July 2026, the startup showcased the test run of its 5 kN (kilo-newton) air-breathing RDE at DRDO’s Defence Research and Development Laboratory (DRDL) facility in Hyderabad. As per the startup, its proof motor exceeded projected thrust despite reduced airflow and completed five ground tests within 24 hours. 

The startup’s pitch rests heavily on cost. Jha claims that D-Propulse can make RDE engines “at least 60% cheaper” than conventional ramjets. However, the estimate is based on projected manufacturing economics and has not yet been validated through commercial production. 

Opening India’s Aerotech Economy 

In the global scramjet market, valued at over $500 Mn in 2025 as per Fortune Business Insights, D-Propulse is eyeing a piece of the nascent RDE opportunity, which is projected to surpass $2.4 Bn by 2030. However, the nascency does not mean there is no competition.

While there is no direct rival on the home turf, GE Aerospace and Lockheed Martin have tested a rotating detonation ramjet on the global front. US-based Venus Aerospace is also pursuing similar tech. 

With many deep-pocketed players vying for the space, compactness and efficiency reflect a broader industry pursuit. D-Propulse’s potential advantage will depend on whether it can translate its design into engines that are cheaper, reliable and suitable for integration into defence platforms. On this front, D-Propulse, which has yet to mint any revenue, has much more planned:

  • A 5,000+ sq ft combustor test facility at IIT Madras, with an air mass flow capacity of around 10 kg/sec and an in-house high-performance computing (HPC) cluster
  • A liquid-hydrocarbon combustion test “soon”
  • Raising a Series A round by early next year 
  • Early flight test planned between June 2027 and December 2027
  • Limited series production by the end of 2028
  • Eyeing Indian Armed Forces as its first intended buyers

Besides, it is also exploring a second, near-term revenue idea: renting out its own infrastructure. For this, the startup is also building domestic testing facilities to reduce reliance on overseas labs, cut testing time and costs, and speed up the development of homegrown jet engines.

Inc42 Take: Can D-Propulse Turn Its Engine Technology Into A Viable Business? 

D-Propulse’s ground tests mark an encouraging technical milestone, but the startup is still far from developing a commercially viable engine. It needs to demonstrate reliable performance in flight, validate its claimed cost and efficiency advantages, and prove that its engines can be manufactured consistently at scale.

Besides, rotating detonation technology alone is not a competitive advantage, with established global aerospace players pursuing similar systems. D-Propulse will need to differentiate itself on performance, pricing and commercial execution.

The startup has yet to secure paying customers. Its proposed testing facility could provide an early revenue stream while its engines undergo further development. However, the facility will also require investment, and its commercial viability will depend on securing sufficient external demand.

For D-Propulse, the next big challenge is moving beyond successful ground tests to engines that meet real-world defence requirements and securing customers willing to pay for them.

item.title: Walmart Probes Flipkart Employees Over Alleged ₹150 Cr Kickbacks: Report
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: US retail giant Walmart has launched an investigation into allegations that employees at its subsidiary Flipkart received over ₹150 Cr…
item.content:encoded:
US retail giant Walmart has launched an investigation into allegations that employees at its subsidiary Flipkart received over ₹150 Cr ($16 Mn) in kickbacks from vendors.

The probe follows whistleblower complaints involving employees in Flipkart’s smartphones and luggage and travel accessories (LTA) divisions, Moneycontrol reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Employees allegedly accepted payments and favours from vendors in exchange for preferential treatment on the ecommerce platform, including greater visibility that helped drive sales.

According to the report, some employees allegedly used Flipkart’s B2B operations to facilitate these arrangements. In the smartphones category, employees allegedly took cuts from vendors when devices moved between businesses.

The investigation is ongoing, and the exact quantum and nature of the alleged wrongdoing are yet to be established, the report added.

Responding to Inc42’s queries, a Flipkart spokesperson said, “Flipkart has robust governance processes and controls and is committed to the highest standards of integrity and compliance. We take any concerns seriously and address them through established processes. We remain committed to ensuring the highest standards of ethical conduct across our business.”

According to Moneycontrol, this is Walmart’s third investigation into alleged financial misconduct at Flipkart in less than three years.

An investigation into employees in the LTA division around two-and-a-half years ago resulted in at least three dismissals. Another probe in the smartphones division around six months ago reportedly found wrongdoing by an employee, who resigned before being dismissed.

Flipkart Grapples With Multiple Challenges

The investigation comes amid senior leadership exits, former employees’ concerns over ESOP liquidity, and uncertainty surrounding Flipkart’s IPO timeline.

At least 14 vice presidents and senior vice presidents have left Flipkart over the past year. These include smartphones VP Kanchan Mishra, product and technology VP Amit Sachan, and corporate tax VP Kamal Chopra.

More than 1,000 former Flipkart Group employees recently approached Walmart’s board, seeking equal access to stock buyback opportunities offered to current employees.

They also sought an extension of the window to exercise their vested stock options and a designated point of contact to address their concerns.

Meanwhile, Flipkart Group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy said in July that the company did not have a timeline for going public. Earlier reports said Walmart had asked Flipkart to prioritise profitability and target EBITDA breakeven by the end of FY27 before pursuing an IPO or another external fundraise.

Flipkart Internet reported an 18% YoY increase in consolidated operating revenue to ₹1,45,880 Cr in FY26. Its consolidated net loss narrowed marginally to ₹8,468 Cr from ₹8,646 Cr in FY25.

These consolidated results reflect the Flipkart Group’s performance, including businesses such as Myntra and Cleartrip, following its redomiciliation to India.

Flipkart also continues to invest in newer businesses, including quick commerce platform Flipkart Minutes, which competes with Blinkit, Zepto, and Swiggy Instamart. The company is also exploring opportunities in food delivery and event ticketing.

item.title: AU SFB Probes Potential Data Leak, Vijay Sales’ Admin Access Allegedly Listed For $25K
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: AU Small Finance Bank (AU SFB) is investigating a potential data leak involving a Salesforce-hosted software platform holding limited information…
item.content:encoded:
AU Small Finance Bank (AU SFB) is investigating a potential data leak involving a Salesforce-hosted software platform holding limited information on its vehicle loan customers, after a hacker group claimed to have accessed sensitive customer and internal records.

The Jaipur-headquartered lender confirmed the investigation, while maintaining that its own systems remain unaffected and all banking services are operating normally.

Separately, a threat actor has allegedly offered administrator access to electronics retailer Vijay Sales’ systems for $25,000. Neither the extent of the alleged access nor the extraction of any data has been independently confirmed.

The AU SFB investigation follows a post flagged by cybersecurity tracking account Hackmanac on X. A group calling itself ScarlettGroup claimed to have breached the lender’s records and threatened to publish the allegedly stolen information.

According to the group, the information includes KYC records, PAN and Aadhaar details, credit reports, bank statements, loan applications, signed agreements, and insurance records.

It also claimed to have accessed customer relationship management (CRM) data, employee information, and audit logs. Inc42 could not independently verify these claims.

“AU Small Finance Bank is investigating a potential data leak involving a software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform managed and hosted by Salesforce, which holds limited data relating to our vehicle loan customers,” a bank spokesperson told ThePrint. “We reaffirm that the Bank’s own systems remain unaffected and all banking services are operating normally.”

The lender did not confirm whether the Salesforce-hosted platform was the source of the data the group claims to hold. It also did not disclose how many customers may have been affected.

AU SFB partnered with Salesforce in 2024 to digitise onboarding for its vehicle loan customers and streamline their journeys. At the time, Bhaskar Karkera, head of retail assets at AU SFB, described Salesforce as the bank’s partner in digitising customer journeys for vehicle loans.

Salesforce customers have previously faced cyberattacks involving social engineering and compromised third-party application connections. In one campaign, attackers used voice phishing to trick employees into connecting malicious applications to corporate Salesforce accounts, potentially exposing customer data.

However, there is no verified evidence linking the AU SFB incident to those campaigns or establishing that Salesforce’s core platform was compromised.

Vijay Sales Access Claim

Separately, an actor using the handle ‘shinymontanna’ claims to be selling super administrator access to Vijay Sales’ internal systems for $25,000, according to a post shared by the X account DarkWeb Informer.

Super administrator access typically gives a user broad control over a system, including the ability to manage other users and their permissions.

The listing claims access to more than 3 Mn order records, information on 15,000 employees, and billing records relating to approximately 1.4 Lakh vendors.

The actor further claims that the access covers customer information, payment and bank transfer records, inventory, financial reports, and internal applications, with permissions to view, modify, and export data.

Screenshots purportedly showing administrative dashboards and super administrator privileges have also been circulated.

However, the claims remain unverified. There is no independent confirmation of the extent of the alleged access or whether any customer or corporate information has been extracted.

Vijay Sales did not respond to Inc42’s queries on the matter.

The developments follow other recent cybersecurity incidents involving customer data exposure and vulnerabilities in digital systems.

Earlier this month, SBI flagged the exposure of 3,897 customer records on the dark web. The records reportedly included personal information such as mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, and residential addresses.

Separately, two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language widely used to build websites, came to light, prompting governments and companies worldwide to take emergency action.

Cybersecurity company eMudhra also recently announced plans to voluntarily wind down its global secure sockets layer and transport layer security (SSL/TLS) certificate business following a certificate security incident.

A researcher found that private keys associated with eight of its intermediate certificate authorities (CAs), which issue digital certificates used to secure website connections, could be recovered.

eMudhra said it revoked all eight affected intermediates and that no certificates had been issued from them. It also said its infrastructure had not been compromised and no data had been breached.

item.content:encoded:
D2C home appliance startup upliance.ai is in advanced talks to raise $3 Mn to $4 Mn (around ₹28-₹37 Cr) in a Series A funding round, sources told Inc42.

A new investor is expected to join the startup’s cap table, while existing backers, including Khosla Ventures, are looking to invest further, the sources said.

The startup could use the fresh capital to strengthen R&D, improve its interface, and expand into international markets, they added.

Inc42 has reached out to upliance.ai for comment. The story will be updated based on the startup’s response.

The startup previously raised ₹34 Cr in a seed funding round led by Khosla Ventures in February 2024, at a valuation of ₹143 Cr (about $15 Mn).

Founded in 2021 by former Ather Energy executive Mahek Mody and former Chaayos employee Mohit Sharma, upliance.ai builds smart kitchen appliances. Its portfolio includes the upliance 2.0+ cooking assistant and a 12L Smart Air Fryer Oven launched in July.

The startup uses generative AI to translate recipes into instructions its cooking assistant can execute. For instance, its YouTube recipe feature breaks cooking videos into steps and maps them to the appliance’s capabilities, including chopping ingredients and adjusting cooking sequences.

In an earlier interaction with Inc42, Mody said customers can also access recipes through the company’s app and leave a voicemail if something goes wrong while cooking. The team responds to these queries and uses ratings and feedback to improve recipes over time. 

The funding talks come amid growing activity in India’s smart kitchen appliances market. According to MarkNtel Advisors, the market is estimated to be worth $800 Mn in 2026 and is projected to reach $2.99 Bn by 2032, growing at a CAGR of 25%. Cooking appliances account for about 48% of the market in 2026.

The segment includes both startups and established appliance brands offering varying degrees of cooking automation.

Wonderchef entered the automated cooking appliance space in April 2024 with the launch of Chef Magic, an all-in-one kitchen robot. The device automates functions such as chopping, stirring, steaming, sautéing and kneading, and comes with an in-built weighing scale, touchscreen interface and more than 600 preloaded recipes.

More recently, Philips launched OneChef in India in March 2026, combining functions such as air frying, stir frying, steaming, and boiling in a single appliance.

item.title: MeitY Floats New Privacy-Led Framework To Unlock Data For Training AI Models
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: The IT ministry (MeitY) has proposed a consent-based framework to facilitate data sharing for training AI models in India.  Called…
item.content:encoded:
The IT ministry (MeitY) has proposed a consent-based framework to facilitate data sharing for training AI models in India. 

Called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI training, the framework aims to help startups, businesses and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets to develop AI models while protecting citizens’ privacy and ensuring compliance with the DPDP Act. 

The DEPA for AI training also proposes a techno-legal architecture to enable organisations to collaborate on AI model training without directly transferring underlying datasets. 

With this, the ministry aims to foster access to datasets for researchers and businesses looking to train AI models. The guidelines have been formulated in collaboration with think tank iSPIRT.

Explaining The New Proposed Framework

The proposed architecture builds on India’s existing DEPA framework, which already supports consent-based data sharing through initiatives such as Account Aggregator. The new framework encompasses the following technical pillars: 

  • Confidential Clean Rooms: Secure computing environments where organisations can collaborate on data processing and AI model training without exposing the underlying datasets to one another
  • Differential Privacy: A privacy-preserving technique used to ensure that individual-level information cannot be identified or extracted from an aggregate dataset
  • Electronic Contracts: Machine-readable agreements that define and enforce data-sharing conditions, including permitted uses, data protection and security requirements
  • Zero-Trust Security: An approach where every access request is authenticated and authorised, with encryption, continuous monitoring and auditing to protect data 

The proposed framework also defines key stakeholders for enabling safe sharing of data for training AI models:

  • Training Data Providers (TDPs): Organisations that make their data accessible through the framework. For instance: banks, hospitals, government agencies 
  • Training Data Consumers (TDCs): Startups, enterprises, researchers and individuals seeking access to datasets to train AI models 
  • Data Collectives or Data Collabs: Intermediaries that aggregate, standardise, and organise data from various sources and define data-sharing policies and governance rules for participants 

Under the DEPA framework, TDPs would first register their datasets on a data exchange platform after anonymising and encrypting them. The datasets would then be tagged with metadata and cryptographic identifiers for traceability. 

TDCs can then request a dataset for their specific use cases, and an electronic contract system checks their requests against data-sharing policies and governance rules before granting access. 

Once access is given, the model is then trained within a secure data environment using differential privacy methods, ensuring that the raw data remains inaccessible to consumers. 

The framework also proposes that trained models must undergo independent checks for bias, fairness, security, safety and explainability. Only models that pass receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling. 

Even after deployment, the oversight will continue in the interest of long-term trust and accountability. In line with this, the framework will ensure that TDCs remain subject to continuous monitoring, periodic reviews, and traceability of the model’s outputs back to the data and contracts used in its training. 

Govt’s Focus On AI Governance

The launch of the new DEPA framework for AI training comes soon after TRAI also released draft guidelines on the responsible use of AI in telecom networks and service delivery. The telecom regulator has sought inputs from stakeholders by November 27. 

As per TRAI, its draft guidelines are rooted in the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines. The centre had earlier released these guidelines to focus on fostering innovation and safe development and deployment of AI offerings, while mitigating risks posed by the technology. 

A few weeks ago, union IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw had also said that the centre will release a consultation paper for regulation on AI safety and security within a month. Earlier reports had also hinted that the Centre was looking at formulating a new framework for AI regulation.

item.content:encoded:
Update | Oct 30, 19:55 IST

The Competition Commission of India (CCI) has cleared Prosus’ investment in Navi to acquire a minority interest in the IPO-bound fintech company.

“The Target is the holding company of the Navi Group, which offers financial services accessible through a single consumer-facing mobile app. The Target offers transparent, user-friendly financial products through its subsidiaries, all accessible via mobile devices,” the CCI said.

 

Original | Aug 19, 18:54 IST

Global VC firm Prosus has invested $100 Mn (over ₹955 Cr) in Sachin Bansal-led fintech startup Navi, marking the latter’s first institutional capital raise.

The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals, including clearance from the Competition Commission of India (CCI), Navi said in a statement.

The fintech startup did not disclose the valuation at which Prosus is making the investment, the stake the investor will acquire, or how it plans to deploy the fresh capital.

“My association with Naspers and the Prosus Group dates back more than a decade, making this partnership particularly meaningful. Their investment is a strong endorsement of the institution we’re building at Navi,” cofounder and executive chairman Bansal said.

In a statement, Navi said that it is entering its next phase of growth with strong operating momentum across its businesses.

Ashutosh Sharma, head of Prosus India investments and M&A, said the investor was backing Navi on account of its large user base, multiple business lines, and technology-first approach.

“We believe the team has executed extremely well in the last 12 months despite a tough macro environment, which makes the company well-positioned to capture significant opportunities in the sector in times to come,” Sharma added.

During FY26, Navi UPI claims to have strengthened its position as digital payments platforms, while Navi Finserv continued to scale its lending franchise responsibly with AUM crossing ₹13K Cr.

The company also said the Navi Group achieved consolidated profitability in the fourth quarter of FY26 but did not disclose the financial figures.

NBFC arm Navi Finserv’s standalone net profit increased 32% YoY to ₹292.2 Cr in FY26, while its operating revenue rose 8% to ₹2,461 Cr. However, its consolidated net profit declined 46% to ₹93.3 Cr during the year, even as operating revenue grew 17% to ₹2,691.5 Cr.

Navi’s IPO Plans

The investment comes at a time when Navi is reportedly looking to revive its public listing plans. Recent reports suggested that the fintech startup could refile its draft IPO papers with the SEBI by December this year.

Navi is said to be eyeing a fresh issue of around ₹3,000 Cr and has appointed JM Financial, Kotak Mahindra Capital, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan as advisers for the proposed offering.

This would mark Navi’s second attempt to go public. The startup filed its draft papers with SEBI in 2022 for a ₹3,350 Cr IPO but later shelved the plan amid adverse market conditions.

Founded by Bansal and Ankit Agarwal in 2018, Navi offers financial products across lending, insurance, mutual funds, and UPI payments. Bansal stepped down as the startup’s chief executive in February 2025 and took over as its executive chairman.

Navi said its UPI platform retained its position as India’s fourth-largest third-party application provider by transaction volume during FY26. Meanwhile, the assets under management of its lending arm, Navi Finserv, crossed ₹13,000 Cr.

item.title: Jio Platforms Q2 Profit Rises 14% YoY To ₹8,387 Cr, Revenue Up 11%
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Recently listed Jio Platforms reported a net profit of ₹8,387 Cr in Q2 FY27, a 13.7% increase from ₹7,379 Cr…
item.content:encoded:
Recently listed Jio Platforms reported a net profit of ₹8,387 Cr in Q2 FY27, a 13.7% increase from ₹7,379 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, net profit grew 8.0% from ₹7,764 Cr in Q1 FY27.

Operating revenue grew 11.4% YoY and 3.3% QoQ to ₹40,475 Cr in the quarter under review. 

Jio Platforms’ other income jumped 49.5% YoY to ₹978 Cr. Including this, total income increased to ₹41,453 Cr, up 12% from ₹36,986 Cr in Q2 FY26.

Total expenses increased 11.6% YoY to ₹30,194 Cr. Network operating expenses, its largest expense head, increased 3.3% to ₹8,813 Cr. 

The company incurred ₹2,872 Cr in tax expenses in Q2, comprising ₹30 Cr in current tax and ₹2,842 Cr in deferred tax. With no exceptional items, its total comprehensive income for the quarter amounted to ₹8,509 Cr. 

Its Q2 EBITDA grew 16.6% YoY to ₹21,879 Cr, a 4.9% sequential increase. With capex excluded, its EBITDA was ₹15,449 Cr. The company said its EBITDA growth was offset by higher finance costs due to 5G asset capitalisation in March 2026.

“This quarter’s results continue to reflect the strength of our 5G network, and the growing reach of our broadband and digital services,” said Jio’s MD Akash Ambani. 

Jio added 9.1 Mn customers on net to bring its customer base of 542.4 Mn by the end of the quarter. With 300 Mn 5G subscribers, the company claims to be the world’s largest 5G operator outside China. 

Its average revenue per user (ARPU) amounted to ₹218.8 per month, up 3.5% YoY,. as promotional schemes for fixed broadband customers were countered by better subscriber mix and increased usage. Each customer consumed around 44.2 GB of mobile data per month on average. 

Meanwhile, its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL), reported operating revenue of ₹35,307 Cr in the quarter, growing 10.8% YoY driven by sustained subscriber momentum and ARPU increase. Margin expansion enabled it to increase EBITDA by 14.7% YoY to ₹20,505 Cr. 

Jio listed on the bourses after closing its ₹30,213 Cr IPO last week. The IPO, which comprised only a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares, was oversubscribed 22.19X. 

Shares of Jio ended today’s trading session 0.57% higher at ₹1,431.20 apiece on the BSE.
